Which statement is logically equivalent to the conditional statement above?" :question/worked-solution "Let's denote by $A$ and $B$ the following statements:

- $A:$ You don't turn the volume up.

- $B:$ You won't hear what they're saying.

Then, our initial statement can be written as $A⇒B,$ which is logically equivalent to 

$$
¬A∨B.
$$

The negation of $A$ can be written as

- $¬A:$ You turn the volume up.

Therefore, the given statement is logically equivalent to the following:

$\,$ You turn the volume up, or you won't hear what they're saying.

We can write this in more everyday language as follows:

$\,$ Turn the volume up, or you won't hear what they're saying." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-6d4b159f-3c60-5c4b-a838-942cc712f24e"] :db/ensure "d17f8721-9970-54a5-a0a5-023397a542c4" :question/math-academy-id "q-102734" :question/problem "Simplify the statement $¬(¬A∨¬B)⇒¬A.$" :question/worked-solution "First, note that

$$
¬(¬A∨¬B)⇒¬A≡¬(¬(¬A∨¬B))∨¬A.
$$

Canceling out double negations, we reach

$$
¬(¬(¬A∨¬B))∨¬A≡(¬A∨¬B)∨¬A.
$$

Using the commutative and associative law, we have

$$
(¬A∨¬B)∨¬A≡(¬A∨¬A)∨¬B.
$$

Finally, by the idempotent law, we have

$$
(¬A∨¬A)∨¬B≡¬A∨¬B.
$$

So the given statement is equivalent to $¬A∨¬B.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-dd4d4d26-9774-5101-8a1e-2da3a880ab36"] :db/ensure The line shown above passes through the points $(0,3)$ and $(-2,-1).$ What is the equation of the line?" :question/worked-solution "We will write the equation of the line in the slope-intercept form $y=mx+b.$ So we need to work out the slope $m$ and the $y$-intercept $b.$

From the graph, we see that the line intercepts the $y$-axis at $(0,3).$ So, the $y$-intercept is $b=3.$

We can calculate the slope of the line by choosing two points on the line and applying the slope formula. The line passes through the points $(0,3)$ and $(-2,-1),$ so we calculate its slope as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}} \\  & =\frac{-1-3}{-2-0} \\  & =\frac{-4}{-2} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the slope $m=2$ and the $y$-intercept $b=3$ into the slope-intercept form $y=mx+b,$ we obtain the equation of the line:

$$
y=2x+3
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-bd5cb081-453f-5660-95d6-9625673b4cec"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id The inequality specifies every number $12z+7$ whose distance from zero is greater than or equal to $5.$ This corresponds to the following compound inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}12z+7 & \le -5 & \text{or} &  & 12z+7 & \ge 5\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve each inequality using the usual methods.

$$
\begin{aligned}12z+7 & \le -5 &  &  & 12z+7 & \ge 5 \\ 12z & \le -12 &  &  & 12z & \ge -2 \\ z & \le -1 &  &  & z & \ge -\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the final solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}z & \le -1 & \text{or} &  & z & \ge -\frac{1}{6}.\end{aligned}

:question/id #uuid "46ac0cd5-cca2-5b10-8e71-7bc6828cb573" :question/math-academy-id "q-156126" :question/problem "What is the solution to the following system of inequalities?

$$
\{\begin{aligned}p-2>3 \\ 1-2p\le -7\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "To solve the system, we need to find the values of $p$ that satisfy both $p-2>3$ and $1-2p\le -7$ simultaneously.

- First, we solve $p-2>3\,:$

$$

{{field-1}}$\text{mg}$" :question/worked-solution "We start by recalling the conversion table for mass units. 

| Name | Symbol | Conversion |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kilogram | $\text{kg}$ | $1\,\text{kg}=1\,000\,\text{g}$ |
| Gram | $\text{g}$ | Base Unit |
| Milligram | $\text{mg}$ | $1\,000\,\text{mg}=1\,\text{g}$ |

$$

$$

There are $1\,000\,\text{mg}$ per $\text{g},$ which we can write as follows:

$$
\frac{1000\,\text{mg}}{\text{g}}
$$

This is our conversion factor.

Now, multiplying $0.9\,\text{g}$ by our conversion factor, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}0.9\,\text{g} & =0.9\,\text{g}\cdot \frac{1\,000\,\text{mg}}{\text{g}} \\  & =0.9\,\cancel{\text{g}}\cdot \frac{1\,000\,\text{mg}}{\cancel{\text{g}}} \\  & =0.9\cdot 1\,000\,\text{mg} \\  & =900\,\text{mg}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $0.9\,\text{g}$ is equivalent to $900\,\text{mg}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-250a40f4-0b82-5e29-a71e-46fe4615e2b3"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-250a40f4-0b82-5e29-a71e-46fe4615e2b3" :answer-field/id #uuid "250a40f4-0b82-5e29-a71e-46fe4615e2b3" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-98aaef27-e9c7-59f1-9e36-1b5d0f4406ec" :answer-field/choices ["answer-98aaef27-e9c7-59f1-9e36-1b5d0f4406ec"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-98aaef27-e9c7-59f1-9e36-1b5d0f4406ec" :answer/id #uuid "98aaef27-e9c7-59f1-9e36-1b5d0f4406ec" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "900" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186105740 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-0a6c019b-459a-54b3-94ee-3cfc489e4bfd"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-0a6c019b-459a-54b3-94ee-3cfc489e4bfd" :question/id #uuid "0a6c019b-459a-54b3-94ee-3cfc489e4bfd" :question/math-academy-id "q-171894" :question/problem "![](images/71/71434714d4941799da3859979b9a75950994efef09b523da00a6a11523e3b906.png)

:question/problem "A triangle has sides $m$, $n$, and $o.$ The sides $m$, $n$, and $o$ are of lengths  $2$, $5$, and $6$, respectively. What is the measure of the angle between the sides $n$ and $o?$ Round your answer to two decimal places." :question/worked-solution "The following triangle illustrates the information given.

![](images/26/26f2041aec84bb0086e2f08c2ba3a19331895951782b7fda153858643a8a5dd4.png)

We use the Law of Cosines to solve for angle $M:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡M & =\frac{{o}^{2}+{n}^{2}-{m}^{2}}{2no}.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Here, we have

$$
m=2,\,n=5,\,o=6.
$$

This gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡M & =\frac{{6}^{2}+{5}^{2}-{2}^{2}}{2(5)(6)} \\  & =\frac{36+25-4}{60} \\  & =\frac{57}{60}.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠M & =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{57}{60}) \\  & ={18.19}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to two decimal places." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-fe46b4b1-2f2f-5fb3-9e1d-afbfc19fa446"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} respectively. If the angle $K$ between $j$ and $l$ has a measure of ${121}^{∘}$, what is the length of side $k?$ Round your answer to two decimal places." :question/worked-solution "The following triangle illustrates the information given.

![](images/1f/1fde3029f6a50388ebd342dc4d15e9787567461b651c24cd6bd6843521b0465d.png)

The Law of Cosines states that

$$
{k}^{2}={j}^{2}+{l}^{2}-2jl\operatorname{cos}⁡K.
$$

Here, we have

$$
m∠K={121}^{∘},\,j=4,\,l=7.
$$

Substituting the numbers into the formula gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{k}^{2} & ={4}^{2}+{7}^{2}-2(4)(7)\operatorname{cos}⁡{121}^{∘} \\  & =16+49-56\operatorname{cos}⁡{121}^{∘} \\  & =65-56(-0.515\,03…) \\  & =65+28.842\,13 \\  & =93.842\,13\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $5$ decimal places. 

Taking the square root gives

$$
k=\sqrt{93.842\,13}=9.69
$$

rounded to two decimal places." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e61d7995-875b-5a12-bc2c-d4a1dc9575fb"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} $$
det(MN)=det(M)\cdot det(N).
$$

In our case, this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =det\begin{bmatrix}4 & -6 & 5 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{bmatrix}\cdot det\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -5 & -2 & 0 \\ 6 & 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that both matrices are triangular. Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =(4\cdot (-2)\cdot 5)\cdot (1\cdot (-2)\cdot 1) \\  & =(-40)\cdot (-2) \\  & =80.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-c090ec9d-391d-5fc2-a3e8-fc77e254c9bb"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id In our case, this gives

$$
det(A)=det\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot det\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 \\ -2 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

We can compute the required determinants as follows:

- For the first determinant, we can compute it using a Laplace expansion down the $2$nd column.

- For the second determinant, we can compute it using a Laplace expansion across the $3$rd row.

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}\cdot \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 \\ -2 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(-1)(-1)^{2+2}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix}\cdot 2(-1)^{3+3}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -2 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-(1-2)\cdot 2(1+2) \\  & =1\cdot 6 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-24bab1b2-9f01-5a84-84a1-c134dbb4356a"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id For example, consider the diagram shown below.

![](images/b7/b7fad622207f396145e930cf74f7905104bf12fa394a9f2f4f5d7ce761cc8e36.png)

The point $A$ has coordinates $(2,3).$ We also have the point $O(0,0)$ that is called the **origin**. 

The vector $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf{a}$ is called the **position vector** of $A.$ A position vector always has its tail at the origin. 

Now let's define two special unit vectors $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j},$ where $|\, \mathbf{i} \,| = |\, \mathbf{j} \,| = 1,$ as follows:

- $\mathbf{i}$ is a horizontal unit vector that points to the right along the positive direction of the $x$-axis, while

- $\mathbf{j}$ is a vertical unit vector that points upwards along the positive direction of the $y$-axis.

These vectors are shown in the picture below. 

![](images/cb/cb5694945b6f76f14a4e66b854f5daa56f3e607bd5b24c4f361ed844dbf8ff7e.png)

We have 

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{OX}=2i, \\  & \overset{\to }{XA}=\overset{\to }{OY}=3j.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, from $\triangle OXA,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OA} & =\overset{\to }{OX}+\overset{\to }{XA} \\  & =2i+3j.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the point $A$ with coordinates $(2,3)$ has a position vector

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OA} & =2i+3j.\end{aligned}
$$

In general, if a point $A$ has coordinates $(a_x,a_y),$ then its position vector is given by

$$
\overrightarrow{OA} = \mathbf{a} = a_x\mathbf{i}+a_y\mathbf{j}.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186101947 :tutorial/content "The $\mathbf{i,j}$ notation can sometimes be cumbersome. An alternative is to use **angle bracket** notation. For example, using angle bracket notation, the vector $2\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}$ can be expressed as

$$
2\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}=\langle 2,3 \rangle.
$$

Note that, using angle bracket notation, the special unit vectors can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}i &=1i+0j=⟨1,0⟩, \\ j &=0i+1j=⟨0,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We can also use **column vector** notation, which is similar to angle bracket notation but expresses the vector as a column rather than a row. For example, using column vector notation, the vector $2\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}$ can be expressed as

![](images/24/2419e5c69bef2cc15f00106e4bf83a17ab2277ed5ea43e8b17f904ca6318873f.svg)

Using column vector notation, the special unit vectors can be expressed as ![](images/f5/f51854ec5bb92b38e5078cfe96046535f8e8efecf1304ea5cc4605dddec09573.svg) and ![](images/ff/ff6013f4f80815a7ca97b5ba8929c2d39b2a4e0165cbb5a8534d8ffafc4377e8.svg)

**Note:** Sometimes, the round bracket notation $(\ldots)$ is used to denote vectors. However, we will avoid using that notation here, because it also looks like the coordinates of a point. A point and its position vector are two separate objects!" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186101948 :tutorial/content "If $A$ and $B$ are points in the Cartesian plane with position vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ respectively, then

$$
\overrightarrow{AB} = \mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}.
$$

To understand why the equation above is true, remember that $\overrightarrow{OA} = \mathbf{a}$ and $\overrightarrow{OB} = \mathbf{b}.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =\overset{\to }{AO}+\overset{\to }{OB} \\  & =-\overset{\to }{OA}+\overset{\to }{OB} \\  & =-a+b \\  & =b-a.\end{aligned}
$$

For example, given $A(5,13)$ and $B(-2,-35)$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{OA}=a=5i+13j, \\  & \overset{\to }{OB}=b=-2i-35j.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =b-a \\  & =(-2i-35j)-(5i+13j) \\  & =-7i-48j.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186101032 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186100920 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-e56f348b-304a-594f-855c-44aa9e7abb11" "question-0f8b5f6f-ca62-5fd3-b5bd-ae649230f08c"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-e56f348b-304a-594f-855c-44aa9e7abb11" :question/id #uuid "e56f348b-304a-594f-855c-44aa9e7abb11" :question/math-academy-id "q-16096" :question/problem "The values of functions $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ and their derivatives at $x=-4$ are given in the table below.

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =a{y}^{3}{e}^{x-1}+3{x}^{2}{e}^{y-1}, \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & ={x}^{3}{e}^{y-1}+3b{y}^{2}{e}^{x-1}, \\ {f}_{x}(1,1) & =4.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the mixed partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{x}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(a{y}^{3}{e}^{x-1}+3{x}^{2}{e}^{y-1}) \\  & =3a{y}^{2}{e}^{x-1}+3{x}^{2}{e}^{y-1} \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{y}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}{e}^{y-1}+3b{y}^{2}{e}^{x-1}) \\  & =3{x}^{2}{e}^{y-1}+3b{y}^{2}{e}^{x-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. Hence, we have the identity

$$
\begin{aligned}3a{y}^{2}{e}^{x-1}+3{x}^{2}{e}^{y-1} &=3{x}^{2}{e}^{y-1}+3b{y}^{2}{e}^{x-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of ${y}^{2}{e}^{x-1},$ respectively, we see that $a=b.$ 

Since ${f}_{x}(1,1)=4$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,1) & =4 \\ a(1)^{3}{e}^{0}+3(1)^{2}{e}^{0} & =4 \\ a+3 & =4 \\ a & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
b=a=1.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-cb13aea9-bc77-5453-9aea-bf5b7e71380f"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Find the values of $a$ and $b$, if 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =2ax{y}^{2}-4xy+15x, \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =b{x}^{2}y-2{x}^{2}-4y, \\ {f}_{y}(-1,-1) & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the mixed partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{x}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2ax{y}^{2}-4xy+15x) \\  & =4axy-4x-0 \\  & =4axy-4x \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{y}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(b{x}^{2}y-2{x}^{2}-4y) \\  & =2bxy-4x-0 \\  & =2bxy-4x\end{aligned}
$$

Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. Hence, we have the identity

$$
\begin{aligned}4axy-4x &=2bxy-4x.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $xy$, we see that $a=\frac{b}{2}.$ 

Now, since ${f}_{y}(-1,-1)=-5$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(-1,-1) & =-5 \\ b(-1)^{2}(-1)-2(-1)^{2}-4(-1) & =-5 \\ -b-2+4 & =-5 \\ b & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
a=\frac{b}{2}=\frac{7}{2}.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-ff468151-5610-57e8-a342-0015e9de243b"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-0032ce9b-c24d-5a4a-8814-0479ffd35234" :question/id #uuid "0032ce9b-c24d-5a4a-8814-0479ffd35234" :question/math-academy-id "q-80840" :question/problem "Suppose that a function $f(x,y,z)$ and all of its higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ and that

$$
{f}_{zx}(x,y,z)=-\frac{2yz}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},\,{f}_{yz}(x,y,z)=\frac{2xz}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$

 

Evaluate the following expression at the point $(1,2,1):$

$$
{f}_{zyy}(x,y,z)+{f}_{xxz}(x,y,z)
$$" :question/worked-solution "As the higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. 

Hence, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{zyy}(x,y,z) & ={f}_{yzy}(x,y,z) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{yz}(x,y,z)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{2xz}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}) \\  & =-\frac{4xyz}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In addition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xxz}(x,y,z) & ={f}_{zxx}(x,y,z) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{zx}(x,y,z)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-\frac{2yz}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{4xyz}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the above, we get

$$
{f}_{zyy}(x,y,z)+{f}_{xxz}(x,y,z)=-\frac{4xyz}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})^{2}}+\frac{4xyz}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})^{2}}=0.
$$

Finally, 

$$
{f}_{zyy}(1,2,1)+{f}_{xxz}(1,2,1)=0.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-94c40397-9482-5a52-b940-12d808c2acb6"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id #uuid "8db2f83d-f6c6-583a-9190-f65543a5bd2c" :question/math-academy-id "q-138836" :question/problem "Consider the function $y=\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{({x}^{2}-2x-8)^{2}}.$ The derivative of this function is given by

$$
{y}^{′}=\frac{2{e}^{{x}^{2}}g(x)}{({x}^{2}-2x-8)^{3}}.
$$

Find the function $g(x).$" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y=\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{({x}^{2}-2x-8)^{2}}.
$$

First, we find the natural logarithm of both sides and use the quotient and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{({x}^{2}-2x-8)^{2}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{{x}^{2}})-\operatorname{ln}⁡{({x}^{2}-2x-8)}^{2} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & ={x}^{2}-2\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-2x-8)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}-2\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-2x-8)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =2x-2\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{2}-2x-8}\cdot (2x-2) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =2x-\frac{4x-4}{{x}^{2}-2x-8}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(2x-\frac{4x-4}{{x}^{2}-2x-8})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{({x}^{2}-2x-8)^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{({x}^{2}-2x-8)^{2}}(2x-\frac{4x-4}{{x}^{2}-2x-8}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{({x}^{2}-2x-8)^{2}}(\frac{2x({x}^{2}-2x-8)-(4x-4)}{{x}^{2}-2x-8}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{({x}^{2}-2x-8)^{3}}(2x({x}^{2}-2x-8)-(4x-4)) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{({x}^{2}-2x-8)^{3}}(2{x}^{3}-4{x}^{2}-16x-4x+4) \\  & =\frac{2{e}^{{x}^{2}}({x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}-10x+2)}{({x}^{2}-2x-8)^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore,

$$

"Evaluate the following limit:

${lim}_{n\to 0}{(1+n)}^{4/7n}=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Notice that as $n\to 0,$ 

- the expression inside the parentheses approaches $1,$ while

- the exponent approaches $\infty .$

So, if we attempt to evaluate the limit directly, we get

$$
{lim}_{n\to 0}{(1+n)}^{4/7n}={1}^{\infty },
$$

which is an indeterminate form.

Instead, let's recall the following special limit:

$$
{lim}_{n\to 0}{(1+n)}^{1/n}=e
$$

Rewriting the given limit using the algebra of limits and applying our special limit, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{n\to 0}{(1+n)}^{4/7n} & ={lim}_{n\to 0}{[{(1+n)}^{1/n}]}^{4/7} \\  & ={[{lim}_{n\to 0}{(1+n)}^{1/n}]}^{4/7} \\  & ={e}^{4/7} \\  & =\sqrt[7]{{e}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-7e129902-6deb-5f56-af1c-12c6f695aaf0"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-7e129902-6deb-5f56-af1c-12c6f695aaf0" :answer-field/id #uuid "7e129902-6deb-5f56-af1c-12c6f695aaf0" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-cb4fd080-504f-597c-84bf-48ecf4885982" :answer-field/choices ["answer-cb4fd080-504f-597c-84bf-48ecf4885982"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-cb4fd080-504f-597c-84bf-48ecf4885982" :answer/id #uuid "cb4fd080-504f-597c-84bf-48ecf4885982" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "e^{\frac{4}{7}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186096836 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-8f2aebee-176b-5447-94e6-cdb44a5559c2"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-8f2aebee-176b-5447-94e6-cdb44a5559c2" :question/id #uuid "8f2aebee-176b-5447-94e6-cdb44a5559c2" :question/math-academy-id "q-351023" :question/problem "Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.

${\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})\,\text{d}x=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "First, we write the integral as

$$
{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})\,\text{d}x={\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}x.
$$

 

We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{3}{x} \\ {v}^{′}=1\, & ⟹\,v=\int 1\cdot \,dx=x\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}u{v}^{′}\text{d}x \\  & =uv{|}_{1}^{{e}^{2}}-{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}v{u}^{′}\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})\,(x){|}_{1}^{{e}^{2}}-{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}x(\frac{3}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =[\operatorname{ln}⁡(({e}^{2})^{3})\,({e}^{2})-\operatorname{ln}⁡({1}^{3})\,(1)]-3{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{6})-3x{|}_{1}^{{e}^{2}} \\  & =6{e}^{2}-3({e}^{2}-1) \\  & =3({e}^{2}+1).\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-8946e118-e7e3-5ee7-9e3c-9199dfb40a0e"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-8946e118-e7e3-5ee7-9e3c-9199dfb40a0e" :answer-field/id #uuid "8946e118-e7e3-5ee7-9e3c-9199dfb40a0e" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-4245b790-1a22-59f1-b2b1-ec25d43743c0" :answer-field/choices ["answer-4245b790-1a22-59f1-b2b1-ec25d43743c0"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4245b790-1a22-59f1-b2b1-ec25d43743c0" :answer/id #uuid "4245b790-1a22-59f1-b2b1-ec25d43743c0" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3({e}^{2}+1)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078407 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-0c781737-7cc2-58de-b406-ca857cb292ed"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-0c781737-7cc2-58de-b406-ca857cb292ed" :question/id #uuid "0c781737-7cc2-58de-b406-ca857cb292ed" :question/math-academy-id "q-339011" :question/problem "Find the value of $a$ given that

$$
{lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{(\frac{1}{a+h}-\frac{1}{a})}{h}=-\frac{1}{4}\,.
$$

$a=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "First, we let 

$$
L=\frac{(\frac{1}{a+h}-\frac{1}{a})}{h}=-\frac{1}{4}.
$$

Comparing this with the formula for the instantaneous rate of change,

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h},
$$

we see that if we let $f(x)=\frac{1}{x}$, we get

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{(\frac{1}{a+h}-\frac{1}{a})}{h}=L.
$$

This confirms that $L={f}^{′}(a).$

Computing the derivative, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}},\,{f}^{′}(a)=-\frac{1}{{a}^{2}},
$$

and so,  $L=-\frac{1}{{a}^{2}}.$

Finally, since $L=-\frac{1}{4},$ we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{{a}^{2}} & =-\frac{1}{4} \\ {a}^{2} & =4 \\ a & =\pm 2.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-566ccb36-6055-535a-bafd-ee2a268c69a1"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id :question/worked-solution "First, let's sketch the graph of  $y=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{4})+\pi :$

$$

$\mathbf{a} = \langle 2,3 \rangle$ and $\mathbf{b} = \langle -4,4 \rangle,$ shown below. How do we compute the vectors $\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}$  and  $-5\mathbf{a}$ in terms of the standard basis $\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}?$

![](images/25/254809cbc834b493759a6fa09222a2c90c5fbfc3280d22e82470e760a7a4c508.png)

To compute $\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b},$ we collect all of the $\mathbf{i}$'s and $\mathbf{j}$'s. We know that $\mathbf{a} = {\color{red}2}\mathbf{i} + {\color{blue}3}\mathbf{j}$ and $\mathbf{b} = {\color{red}-4}\mathbf{i} + {\color{blue}4}\mathbf{j}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b & =(2i+3j)+(-4i+4j) \\  & =(2+(-4))i+(3+4)j \\  & =-2i+7j.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing our answer in angle bracket and column vector notations, we get 
![](images/ea/eae25a74dde73f7899f6ccbbdbb1a1f589fc72cad9629a33b4fdbbbc753efcd8.svg)

To compute $-5\mathbf{a},$ we multiply each of the components by $-5\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}-5\cdot a & =-5(2i+3j) \\  & =(-5\cdot 2)i+(-5\cdot 3)j \\  & =-10i+-15j\end{aligned}
$$

Writing our answer in angle bracket and column vector notations, we get 
![](images/05/05f847a73201db3de20db3847ef4ed97e07ea7fae9325401b1ea5a460968f9da.svg)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186060908 :tutorial/content "To add or subtract vectors given in angle bracket or column vector form, we just need to add or subtract each component separately.

For example, in angle bracket notation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨2,5⟩+⟨-3,7⟩ & = \\ ⟨2+(-3),5+7⟩ & = \\ ⟨-1,12⟩ & ,\end{aligned}
$$

and in column vector notation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 7\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2+(-3) \\ 5+7\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 12\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Likewise, to multiply a vector given in angle bracket or column vector form, we just need to multiply each component separately.

For example, in angle bracket notation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-5\cdot ⟨2,5⟩ & = \\ ⟨(-5)\cdot 2,(-5)\cdot 5⟩ & = \\ ⟨-10,-25⟩ & ,\end{aligned}
$$

and in column vector notation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-5\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 5\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}(-5)\cdot 2 \\ (-5)\cdot 5\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-10 \\ -25\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186060909 :tutorial/content "To denote a vector, we have used two notations:

- a single bold lowercase letter, such as $\mathbf{v},$ or

- two uppercase letters representing the points of the ends of the vector, with an arrow over them, such as $\overrightarrow{AB}.$

We will mostly stick to these notations. However, there are many possible notations for vectors. For example, sometimes a vector can be denoted as

$$
\vec{v}, \quad \overrightarrow{V}, \quad v, \quad \hat{v}.
$$

The rightmost notation, $\hat{v},$ is usually used to represent unit vectors in particular." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186059922 :activity/expected-seconds 540.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054746 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-070008c9-e913-5456-a5af-e255c5aba081" "question-2e637b5f-6f34-5a1c-b2e1-f9ed9e9b050b"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-070008c9-e913-5456-a5af-e255c5aba081" :question/id #uuid "070008c9-e913-5456-a5af-e255c5aba081" :question/math-academy-id "q-30824" :question/problem "${log}_{64}⁡(\sqrt{8})=$" :question/worked-solution "We use the change of base formula:

$$

In our case, $a=64$ and $X=\sqrt{8}.$ Since both $a$ and $X$ can be presented as a power of $8,$ we set $b=8.$ So, we have:

$$
P=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -2\end{bmatrix}?
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to convert $P$ to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Looking at the row echelon form, we see that $P$ has $3$ pivots. In particular, the pivot columns are the $1$st, $3$rd, and $4$th columns." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields "![](images/cf/cf7890789d1b80002ac2055fd61e8c8f58525f9bb1714bd77ff6e8542567e962.png)

Let $A(-2,0)$ and $B(3,3).$ Find $|\overset{\to }{AB}|.$ Do not round the answer.

$|\overset{\to }{AB}|=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We have 

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{OA}=a=-2i+0j, \\  & \overset{\to }{OB}=b=3i+3j.\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing $\overset{\to }{AB}$ as the difference of position vectors, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =\overset{\to }{OB}-\overset{\to }{OA} \\  & =b-a \\  & =(3i+3j)-(-2i+0j) \\  & =5i+3j.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the formula for the magnitude of a vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|\overset{\to }{AB}| & =\sqrt{{5}^{2}+{3}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25+9} \\  & =\sqrt{34}.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =\frac{3r+2s}{|3r+2s|}\end{aligned}
$$

First, let's compute the sum:

$$
\begin{aligned}3r+2s & =3\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+2\cdot \begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}(-6)+0 \\ 3+(-6)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula for the magnitude of a vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|3r+2s| & =\sqrt{(-6)^{2}+(-3)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{45} \\  & =3\sqrt{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide $3r+2s$ by its length and get the following unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =\frac{3r+2s}{|3r+2s|} \\  & =\frac{1}{3\sqrt{5}}(3r+2s) \\  & =\frac{1}{3\sqrt{5}}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-6 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-486b8f01-6945-5809-91a8-88d9d6a85f09"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $\mathbf{a}=\langle -2,4 \rangle$ shown below.

![](images/cd/cd458eeb41ee09d6a4f58bc343575d46e3d362dc3edca40a47e1a7381fcc9bd2.png)

Expressed in component form, our vector is $\mathbf{a}=-2\mathbf{i} + 4 \mathbf{j}.$

To find the magnitude (length) of $\mathbf{a},$ we can use the Pythagorean theorem on $\triangle OXA.$

The legs of the triangle have lengths

$$
\begin{aligned}|\overset{\to }{OX}| & =|-2|=2\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}|\overset{\to }{XA}| & =|\,4\,|=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the Pythagorean theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\,a\,| & =\sqrt{|\overset{\to }{OX}{|}^{2}+|\overset{\to }{XA}{|}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{5}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186060911 :tutorial/content "We just saw that the magnitude of the vector $\mathbf{a}=\langle -2,4 \rangle$ was given by

$$
\begin{aligned}|\,a\,| & =\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

In general, given a vector
![](images/10/10fbddb6dc3528629e5583ad25976d049ca2ec5943ce3e689953f79299b8afcd.svg)
the magnitude of the vector can always be computed as

$$
|\,\mathbf{a}\,| = \sqrt{a_x^2+a_y^2}.
$$

**Note**

$$
¬[(R⇒¬S)∧(¬S⇒R)]≡¬[(¬R∨¬S)∧(¬¬S∨R)]
$$

Next, we simplify the double negations:

$$
¬[(¬R∨¬S)∧(¬¬S∨R)]≡¬[(¬R∨¬S)∧(S∨R)]

$$
\begin{aligned}¬[(¬R∨¬S)∧(S∨R)] & ≡¬(¬R∨¬S)∨¬(S∨R) \\  & ≡(¬¬R∧¬¬S)∨¬(S∨R)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we again simplify the double negations and write down symbols in alphabetic order inside the parentheses using commutative laws:

$$
\begin{aligned}(¬¬R∧¬¬S)∨¬(S∨R) & ≡(R∧S)∨¬(S∨R) \\  & ≡(R∧S)∨¬(R∨S)\end{aligned}

"Which of the following matrices are transformed into the $2\times 2$ identity matrix after applying the row operations ${R}_{1}↔{R}_{2}\,$ and $\,{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1}?$  

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix},\,B=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 3 \\ 3 & 0\end{bmatrix},\,C=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 3 \\ 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's apply the operations to each of the matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & ↔{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 3 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =I\,✓ \\ B & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 3 \\ 3 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & ↔{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 3 & 3\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ -6 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & \ne I\,\times  \\ C & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 3 \\ 1 & 3\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & ↔{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 3\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 0 & -6\end{bmatrix} \\  & \ne I\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

"The inverse of the $2\times 2$ matrix $P$ is found using row operations, as shown below. Complete the process, and determine ${P}^{-1}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}[P\,|\,I] & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :=-\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -\frac{1}{3} & -\frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -\frac{1}{3} & -\frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{5}{3} & \frac{2}{3} & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{3}{5}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -\frac{1}{3} & -\frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{2}{5} & \frac{3}{5}\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :=\text{___________} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{\phantom{a}} & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{\phantom{a}} \\ 0 & 1 & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{\phantom{a}} & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{\phantom{a}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "We write down $P$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply the standard Gauss-Jordan method to transform the matrix $P$ into the identity matrix. We perform the same row operations on both matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}[P\,|\,I] & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :=-\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -\frac{1}{3} & -\frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -\frac{1}{3} & -\frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{5}{3} & \frac{2}{3} & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{3}{5}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -\frac{1}{3} & -\frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{2}{5} & \frac{3}{5}\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & -\frac{1}{5} & \frac{1}{5} \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{2}{5} & \frac{3}{5}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The matrix ${P}^{-1}$ is given by the right-hand side of our big matrix after all of the transformations have been completed. Therefore, 

$$
{P}^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{5} & \frac{1}{5} \\ \frac{2}{5} & \frac{3}{5}\end{bmatrix}.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-8cea2ad4-e0cc-5ef8-b8e2-86f20e8d1d7a"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id The inequality specifies every number $12z+7$ whose distance from zero is greater than or equal to $5.$ This corresponds to the following compound inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}12z+7 & \le -5 & \text{or} &  & 12z+7 & \ge 5\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve each inequality using the usual methods.

$$
\begin{aligned}12z+7 & \le -5 &  &  & 12z+7 & \ge 5 \\ 12z & \le -12 &  &  & 12z & \ge -2 \\ z & \le -1 &  &  & z & \ge -\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the final solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}z & \le -1 & \text{or} &  & z & \ge -\frac{1}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-bf84b07b-a308-558a-9ef5-8ba63478514c" "answer-field-07839e3e-5717-5971-8c55-29675d677717" | Name | Symbol | Conversion |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kilogram | $\text{kg}$ | $1\,\text{kg}=1\,000\,\text{g}$ |
| Gram | $\text{g}$ | Base Unit |
| Milligram | $\text{mg}$ | $1\,000\,\text{mg}=1\,\text{g}$ |

$$

$$

There are $1\,000\,\text{mg}$ per $\text{g},$ which we can write as follows:

$$
\frac{1000\,\text{mg}}{\text{g}}
$$

This is our conversion factor.

Now, multiplying $0.9\,\text{g}$ by our conversion factor, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}0.9\,\text{g} & =0.9\,\text{g}\cdot \frac{1\,000\,\text{mg}}{\text{g}} \\  & =0.9\,\cancel{\text{g}}\cdot \frac{1\,000\,\text{mg}}{\cancel{\text{g}}} \\  & =0.9\cdot 1\,000\,\text{mg} \\  & =900\,\text{mg}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $0.9\,\text{g}$ is equivalent to $900\,\text{mg}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-250a40f4-0b82-5e29-a71e-46fe4615e2b3"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-250a40f4-0b82-5e29-a71e-46fe4615e2b3" :answer-field/id #uuid "250a40f4-0b82-5e29-a71e-46fe4615e2b3" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-98aaef27-e9c7-59f1-9e36-1b5d0f4406ec" :answer-field/choices ["answer-98aaef27-e9c7-59f1-9e36-1b5d0f4406ec"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-98aaef27-e9c7-59f1-9e36-1b5d0f4406ec" :answer/id #uuid "98aaef27-e9c7-59f1-9e36-1b5d0f4406ec" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "900" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186105740 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-0a6c019b-459a-54b3-94ee-3cfc489e4bfd"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-0a6c019b-459a-54b3-94ee-3cfc489e4bfd" :question/id #uuid "0a6c019b-459a-54b3-94ee-3cfc489e4bfd" :question/math-academy-id "q-171894" :question/problem "![](images/71/71434714d4941799da3859979b9a75950994efef09b523da00a6a11523e3b906.png)

:question/problem "A triangle has sides $m$, $n$, and $o.$ The sides $m$, $n$, and $o$ are of lengths  $2$, $5$, and $6$, respectively. What is the measure of the angle between the sides $n$ and $o?$ Round your answer to two decimal places." :question/worked-solution "The following triangle illustrates the information given.

![](images/26/26f2041aec84bb0086e2f08c2ba3a19331895951782b7fda153858643a8a5dd4.png)

We use the Law of Cosines to solve for angle $M:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡M & =\frac{{o}^{2}+{n}^{2}-{m}^{2}}{2no}.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Here, we have

$$
m=2,\,n=5,\,o=6.
$$

This gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡M & =\frac{{6}^{2}+{5}^{2}-{2}^{2}}{2(5)(6)} \\  & =\frac{36+25-4}{60} \\  & =\frac{57}{60}.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠M & =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{57}{60}) \\  & ={18.19}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to two decimal places." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-fe46b4b1-2f2f-5fb3-9e1d-afbfc19fa446"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} respectively. If the angle $K$ between $j$ and $l$ has a measure of ${121}^{∘}$, what is the length of side $k?$ Round your answer to two decimal places." :question/worked-solution "The following triangle illustrates the information given.

![](images/1f/1fde3029f6a50388ebd342dc4d15e9787567461b651c24cd6bd6843521b0465d.png)

The Law of Cosines states that

$$
{k}^{2}={j}^{2}+{l}^{2}-2jl\operatorname{cos}⁡K.
$$

Here, we have

$$
m∠K={121}^{∘},\,j=4,\,l=7.
$$

Substituting the numbers into the formula gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{k}^{2} & ={4}^{2}+{7}^{2}-2(4)(7)\operatorname{cos}⁡{121}^{∘} \\  & =16+49-56\operatorname{cos}⁡{121}^{∘} \\  & =65-56(-0.515\,03…) \\  & =65+28.842\,13 \\  & =93.842\,13\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $5$ decimal places. 

Taking the square root gives

$$
k=\sqrt{93.842\,13}=9.69
$$

rounded to two decimal places." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e61d7995-875b-5a12-bc2c-d4a1dc9575fb"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} have

$$
det(MN)=det(M)\cdot det(N).
$$

In our case, this gives

$$
det(A)=det\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot det\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 \\ -2 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

We can compute the required determinants as follows:

- For the first determinant, we can compute it using a Laplace expansion down the $2$nd column.

- For the second determinant, we can compute it using a Laplace expansion across the $3$rd row.

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}\cdot \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 \\ -2 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(-1)(-1)^{2+2}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix}\cdot 2(-1)^{3+3}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -2 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-(1-2)\cdot 2(1+2) \\  & =1\cdot 6 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-24bab1b2-9f01-5a84-84a1-c134dbb4356a"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$

$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-ed7ddc08-5f8d-5c40-bda9-117726299567"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-ed7ddc08-5f8d-5c40-bda9-117726299567" :answer-field/id #uuid "ed7ddc08-5f8d-5c40-bda9-117726299567" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-940aeb78-c446-5984-88ec-716288861a2c" :answer-field/choices ["answer-f2e6b0be-7712-5a3d-8735-6c39db9d2f2a" "answer-3e0ba453-1215-5b3d-a7f0-05c27ba16c19" "answer-d383c3fb-fbe1-569b-ac8c-3692a5c7d2e5" "answer-6409fd64-52ae-588b-83ba-95d3807aaa0a" "answer-940aeb78-c446-5984-88ec-716288861a2c"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f2e6b0be-7712-5a3d-8735-6c39db9d2f2a" :answer/id #uuid "f2e6b0be-7712-5a3d-8735-6c39db9d2f2a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2i+j" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3e0ba453-1215-5b3d-a7f0-05c27ba16c19" :answer/id #uuid "3e0ba453-1215-5b3d-a7f0-05c27ba16c19" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "i" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d383c3fb-fbe1-569b-ac8c-3692a5c7d2e5" :answer/id #uuid "d383c3fb-fbe1-569b-ac8c-3692a5c7d2e5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "i+3j" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6409fd64-52ae-588b-83ba-95d3807aaa0a" :answer/id #uuid "6409fd64-52ae-588b-83ba-95d3807aaa0a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "i+j" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-940aeb78-c446-5984-88ec-716288861a2c" :answer/id #uuid "940aeb78-c446-5984-88ec-716288861a2c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "j" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186101946 :tutorial/content "We can use Cartesian coordinates to define vectors in the plane. For example, consider the diagram shown below.

![](images/b7/b7fad622207f396145e930cf74f7905104bf12fa394a9f2f4f5d7ce761cc8e36.png)

The point $A$ has coordinates $(2,3).$ We also have the point $O(0,0)$ that is called the **origin**. 

The vector $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf{a}$ is called the **position vector** of $A.$ A position vector always has its tail at the origin. 

Now let's define two special unit vectors $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j},$ where $|\, \mathbf{i} \,| = |\, \mathbf{j} \,| = 1,$ as follows:

- $\mathbf{i}$ is a horizontal unit vector that points to the right along the positive direction of the $x$-axis, while

- $\mathbf{j}$ is a vertical unit vector that points upwards along the positive direction of the $y$-axis.

These vectors are shown in the picture below. 

![](images/cb/cb5694945b6f76f14a4e66b854f5daa56f3e607bd5b24c4f361ed844dbf8ff7e.png)

We have 

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{OX}=2i, \\  & \overset{\to }{XA}=\overset{\to }{OY}=3j.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, from $\triangle OXA,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OA} & =\overset{\to }{OX}+\overset{\to }{XA} \\  & =2i+3j.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the point $A$ with coordinates $(2,3)$ has a position vector

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OA} & =2i+3j.\end{aligned}
$$

In general, if a point $A$ has coordinates $(a_x,a_y),$ then its position vector is given by

$$
\overrightarrow{OA} = \mathbf{a} = a_x\mathbf{i}+a_y\mathbf{j}.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186101947 :tutorial/content "The $\mathbf{i,j}$ notation can sometimes be cumbersome. An alternative is to use **angle bracket** notation. For example, using angle bracket notation, the vector $2\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}$ can be expressed as

$$
2\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}=\langle 2,3 \rangle.
$$

Note that, using angle bracket notation, the special unit vectors can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}i &=1i+0j=⟨1,0⟩, \\ j &=0i+1j=⟨0,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We can also use **column vector** notation, which is similar to angle bracket notation but expresses the vector as a column rather than a row. For example, using column vector notation, the vector $2\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}$ can be expressed as

![](images/24/2419e5c69bef2cc15f00106e4bf83a17ab2277ed5ea43e8b17f904ca6318873f.svg)

Using column vector notation, the special unit vectors can be expressed as ![](images/f5/f51854ec5bb92b38e5078cfe96046535f8e8efecf1304ea5cc4605dddec09573.svg) and ![](images/ff/ff6013f4f80815a7ca97b5ba8929c2d39b2a4e0165cbb5a8534d8ffafc4377e8.svg)

**Note:** Sometimes, the round bracket notation $(\ldots)$ is used to denote vectors. However, we will avoid using that notation here, because it also looks like the coordinates of a point. A point and its position vector are two separate objects!" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186101948 :tutorial/content "If $A$ and $B$ are points in the Cartesian plane with position vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ respectively, then

$$
\overrightarrow{AB} = \mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}.
$$

To understand why the equation above is true, remember that $\overrightarrow{OA} = \mathbf{a}$ and $\overrightarrow{OB} = \mathbf{b}.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =\overset{\to }{AO}+\overset{\to }{OB} \\  & =-\overset{\to }{OA}+\overset{\to }{OB} \\  & =-a+b \\  & =b-a.\end{aligned}
$$

For example, given $A(5,13)$ and $B(-2,-35)$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{OA}=a=5i+13j, \\  & \overset{\to }{OB}=b=-2i-35j.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =b-a \\  & =(-2i-35j)-(5i+13j) \\  & =-7i-48j.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186101032 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186100920 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-e56f348b-304a-594f-855c-44aa9e7abb11" "question-0f8b5f6f-ca62-5fd3-b5bd-ae649230f08c"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-e56f348b-304a-594f-855c-44aa9e7abb11" :question/id #uuid "e56f348b-304a-594f-855c-44aa9e7abb11" :question/math-academy-id "q-16096" :question/problem "The values of functions $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ and their derivatives at $x=-4$ are given in the table below.

| $x$ | $f(x)$ | $g(x)$ | ${f}^{′}(x)$ | ${g}^{′}(x)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-4$ | $-2$ | $-7$ | $1$ | $10$ |

Compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(f(x)g(x))$ at $x=-4.$" :question/worked-solution "Using the product rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(f(x)g(x))=f(x){g}^{′}(x)+g(x){f}^{′}(x).
$$

At the point where $x=-4$, this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =a{y}^{3}{e}^{x-1}+3{x}^{2}{e}^{y-1}, \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & ={x}^{3}{e}^{y-1}+3b{y}^{2}{e}^{x-1}, \\ {f}_{x}(1,1) & =4.\end{aligned}

$$

Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. Hence, we have the identity

$$
\begin{aligned}3a{y}^{2}{e}^{x-1}+3{x}^{2}{e}^{y-1} &=3{x}^{2}{e}^{y-1}+3b{y}^{2}{e}^{x-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of ${y}^{2}{e}^{x-1},$ respectively, we see that $a=b.$ 

Since ${f}_{x}(1,1)=4$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,1) & =4 \\ a(1)^{3}{e}^{0}+3(1)^{2}{e}^{0} & =4 \\ a+3 & =4 \\ a & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
b=a=1.

that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Find the values of $a$ and $b$, if 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =2ax{y}^{2}-4xy+15x, \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =b{x}^{2}y-2{x}^{2}-4y, \\ {f}_{y}(-1,-1) & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the mixed partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{x}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2ax{y}^{2}-4xy+15x) \\  & =4axy-4x-0 \\  & =4axy-4x \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{y}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(b{x}^{2}y-2{x}^{2}-4y) \\  & =2bxy-4x-0 \\  & =2bxy-4x\end{aligned}
$$

Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. Hence, we have the identity

$$
\begin{aligned}4axy-4x &=2bxy-4x.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $xy$, we see that $a=\frac{b}{2}.$ 

Now, since ${f}_{y}(-1,-1)=-5$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(-1,-1) & =-5 \\ b(-1)^{2}(-1)-2(-1)^{2}-4(-1) & =-5 \\ -b-2+4 & =-5 \\ b & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
a=\frac{b}{2}=\frac{7}{2}.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-ff468151-5610-57e8-a342-0015e9de243b"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-0032ce9b-c24d-5a4a-8814-0479ffd35234" :question/id #uuid "0032ce9b-c24d-5a4a-8814-0479ffd35234" :question/math-academy-id "q-80840" :question/problem "Suppose that a function $f(x,y,z)$ and all of its higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ and that

$$
{f}_{zx}(x,y,z)=-\frac{2yz}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},\,{f}_{yz}(x,y,z)=\frac{2xz}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$

 

Evaluate the following expression at the point $(1,2,1):$

$$
{f}_{zyy}(x,y,z)+{f}_{xxz}(x,y,z)
$$" :question/worked-solution "As the higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. 

Hence, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{zyy}(x,y,z) & ={f}_{yzy}(x,y,z) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{yz}(x,y,z)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{2xz}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}) \\  & =-\frac{4xyz}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In addition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xxz}(x,y,z) & ={f}_{zxx}(x,y,z) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{zx}(x,y,z)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-\frac{2yz}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{4xyz}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the above, we get

$$
{f}_{zyy}(x,y,z)+{f}_{xxz}(x,y,z)=-\frac{4xyz}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})^{2}}+\frac{4xyz}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})^{2}}=0.
$$

Finally, 

$$
{f}_{zyy}(1,2,1)+{f}_{xxz}(1,2,1)=0.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-94c40397-9482-5a52-b940-12d808c2acb6"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id #uuid "8db2f83d-f6c6-583a-9190-f65543a5bd2c" :question/math-academy-id "q-138836" :question/problem "Consider the function $y=\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{({x}^{2}-2x-8)^{2}}.$ The derivative of this function is given by

$$
{y}^{′}=\frac{2{e}^{{x}^{2}}g(x)}{({x}^{2}-2x-8)^{3}}.
$$

Find the function $g(x).$" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y=\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{({x}^{2}-2x-8)^{2}}.
$$

First, we find the natural logarithm of both sides and use the quotient and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{({x}^{2}-2x-8)^{2}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{{x}^{2}})-\operatorname{ln}⁡{({x}^{2}-2x-8)}^{2} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & ={x}^{2}-2\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-2x-8)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}-2\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-2x-8)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =2x-2\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{2}-2x-8}\cdot (2x-2) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =2x-\frac{4x-4}{{x}^{2}-2x-8}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(2x-\frac{4x-4}{{x}^{2}-2x-8})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{({x}^{2}-2x-8)^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{({x}^{2}-2x-8)^{2}}(2x-\frac{4x-4}{{x}^{2}-2x-8}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{({x}^{2}-2x-8)^{2}}(\frac{2x({x}^{2}-2x-8)-(4x-4)}{{x}^{2}-2x-8}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{({x}^{2}-2x-8)^{3}}(2x({x}^{2}-2x-8)-(4x-4)) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{({x}^{2}-2x-8)^{3}}(2{x}^{3}-4{x}^{2}-16x-4x+4) \\  & =\frac{2{e}^{{x}^{2}}({x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}-10x+2)}{({x}^{2}-2x-8)^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
g(x)={x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}-10x+2.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-0e4c95de-4b57-5003-8261-a6e1c6a6bcc0"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "Evaluate the following limit:

${lim}_{n\to 0}{(1+n)}^{4/7n}=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Notice that as $n\to 0,$ 

- the expression inside the parentheses approaches $1,$ while

- the exponent approaches $\infty .$

So, if we attempt to evaluate the limit directly, we get

$$
{lim}_{n\to 0}{(1+n)}^{4/7n}={1}^{\infty },
$$

which is an indeterminate form.

Instead, let's recall the following special limit:

$$
{lim}_{n\to 0}{(1+n)}^{1/n}=e
$$

Rewriting the given limit using the algebra of limits and applying our special limit, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{n\to 0}{(1+n)}^{4/7n} & ={lim}_{n\to 0}{[{(1+n)}^{1/n}]}^{4/7} \\  & ={[{lim}_{n\to 0}{(1+n)}^{1/n}]}^{4/7} \\  & ={e}^{4/7} \\  & =\sqrt[7]{{e}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-7e129902-6deb-5f56-af1c-12c6f695aaf0"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-7e129902-6deb-5f56-af1c-12c6f695aaf0" :answer-field/id #uuid "7e129902-6deb-5f56-af1c-12c6f695aaf0" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-cb4fd080-504f-597c-84bf-48ecf4885982" :answer-field/choices ["answer-cb4fd080-504f-597c-84bf-48ecf4885982"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-cb4fd080-504f-597c-84bf-48ecf4885982" :answer/id #uuid "cb4fd080-504f-597c-84bf-48ecf4885982" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "e^{\frac{4}{7}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186096836 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-8f2aebee-176b-5447-94e6-cdb44a5559c2"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-8f2aebee-176b-5447-94e6-cdb44a5559c2" :question/id #uuid "8f2aebee-176b-5447-94e6-cdb44a5559c2" :question/math-academy-id "q-351023" :question/problem "Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.

${\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})\,\text{d}x=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "First, we write the integral as

$$
{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})\,\text{d}x={\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}x.
$$

 

We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{3}{x} \\ {v}^{′}=1\, & ⟹\,v=\int 1\cdot \,dx=x\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}u{v}^{′}\text{d}x \\  & =uv{|}_{1}^{{e}^{2}}-{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}v{u}^{′}\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})\,(x){|}_{1}^{{e}^{2}}-{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}x(\frac{3}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =[\operatorname{ln}⁡(({e}^{2})^{3})\,({e}^{2})-\operatorname{ln}⁡({1}^{3})\,(1)]-3{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{6})-3x{|}_{1}^{{e}^{2}} \\  & =6{e}^{2}-3({e}^{2}-1) \\  & =3({e}^{2}+1).\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-8946e118-e7e3-5ee7-9e3c-9199dfb40a0e"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-8946e118-e7e3-5ee7-9e3c-9199dfb40a0e" :answer-field/id #uuid "8946e118-e7e3-5ee7-9e3c-9199dfb40a0e" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-4245b790-1a22-59f1-b2b1-ec25d43743c0" :answer-field/choices ["answer-4245b790-1a22-59f1-b2b1-ec25d43743c0"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4245b790-1a22-59f1-b2b1-ec25d43743c0" :answer/id #uuid "4245b790-1a22-59f1-b2b1-ec25d43743c0" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3({e}^{2}+1)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078407 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-0c781737-7cc2-58de-b406-ca857cb292ed"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-0c781737-7cc2-58de-b406-ca857cb292ed" :question/id #uuid "0c781737-7cc2-58de-b406-ca857cb292ed" :question/math-academy-id "q-339011" :question/problem "Find the value of $a$ given that

$$
{lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{(\frac{1}{a+h}-\frac{1}{a})}{h}=-\frac{1}{4}\,.
$$

$a=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "First, we let 

$$
L=\frac{(\frac{1}{a+h}-\frac{1}{a})}{h}=-\frac{1}{4}.
$$

Comparing this with the formula for the instantaneous rate of change,

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h},
$$

we see that if we let $f(x)=\frac{1}{x}$, we get

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{(\frac{1}{a+h}-\frac{1}{a})}{h}=L.
$$

This confirms that $L={f}^{′}(a).$

Computing the derivative, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}},\,{f}^{′}(a)=-\frac{1}{{a}^{2}},
$$

and so,  $L=-\frac{1}{{a}^{2}}.$

Finally, since $L=-\frac{1}{4},$ we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{{a}^{2}} & =-\frac{1}{4} \\ {a}^{2} & =4 \\ a & =\pm 2.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-566ccb36-6055-535a-bafd-ee2a268c69a1"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id :question/worked-solution "First, let's sketch the graph of  $y=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{4})+\pi :$   

![](images/42/42eb38a11d9d63e05c0078bae4c052566b3162571e8563f22cd52ae31bc6dbd7.png)

The domain of   $\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{4})+\pi$ is $(-\infty ,\infty ).$  

Now, substituting $x=4$ directly into the limit, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{4})+\pi ) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1)+\pi ) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}+\pi ) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{4}) \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-6c3ab6b7-6e70-535c-9a1b-8fc6113a3975"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-6c3ab6b7-6e70-535c-9a1b-8fc6113a3975" :answer-field/id #uuid "6c3ab6b7-6e70-535c-9a1b-8fc6113a3975" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-23691b4e-ef96-59e7-b343-43a0604ca109" :answer-field/choices ["answer-7059fd79-bfc5-56de-bb09-06241fc81d5b" "answer-23691b4e-ef96-59e7-b343-43a0604ca109" "answer-11ddabc6-6948-5d05-984f-8724d78f9060" "answer-8bcb3571-4895-5ea8-a376-01f2897be6f5" "answer-1ac77e93-6655-5cb9-83e2-8d0071ffa65a"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7059fd79-bfc5-56de-bb09-06241fc81d5b" :answer/id #uuid "7059fd79-bfc5-56de-bb09-06241fc81d5b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-23691b4e-ef96-59e7-b343-43a0604ca109" :answer/id #uuid "23691b4e-ef96-59e7-b343-43a0604ca109" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-11ddabc6-6948-5d05-984f-8724d78f9060" :answer/id #uuid "11ddabc6-6948-5d05-984f-8724d78f9060" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8bcb3571-4895-5ea8-a376-01f2897be6f5" :answer/id #uuid "8bcb3571-4895-5ea8-a376-01f2897be6f5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1ac77e93-6655-5cb9-83e2-8d0071ffa65a" :answer/id #uuid "1ac77e93-6655-5cb9-83e2-8d0071ffa65a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-2f397079-49a9-58d1-bc93-fa23602eefa7" :question/id #uuid "2f397079-49a9-58d1-bc93-fa23602eefa7" :question/math-academy-id "q-344566" :question/problem "Evaluate the following limit:

$\mathbf{a} = \langle 2,3 \rangle$ and $\mathbf{b} = \langle -4,4 \rangle,$ shown below. How do we compute the vectors $\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}$  and  $-5\mathbf{a}$ in terms of the standard basis $\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}?$

![](images/25/254809cbc834b493759a6fa09222a2c90c5fbfc3280d22e82470e760a7a4c508.png)

To compute $\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b},$ we collect all of the $\mathbf{i}$'s and $\mathbf{j}$'s. We know that $\mathbf{a} = {\color{red}2}\mathbf{i} + {\color{blue}3}\mathbf{j}$ and $\mathbf{b} = {\color{red}-4}\mathbf{i} + {\color{blue}4}\mathbf{j}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b & =(2i+3j)+(-4i+4j) \\  & =(2+(-4))i+(3+4)j \\  & =-2i+7j.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing our answer in angle bracket and column vector notations, we get 
![](images/ea/eae25a74dde73f7899f6ccbbdbb1a1f589fc72cad9629a33b4fdbbbc753efcd8.svg)

To compute $-5\mathbf{a},$ we multiply each of the components by $-5\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}-5\cdot a & =-5(2i+3j) \\  & =(-5\cdot 2)i+(-5\cdot 3)j \\  & =-10i+-15j\end{aligned}
$$

Writing our answer in angle bracket and column vector notations, we get 
![](images/05/05f847a73201db3de20db3847ef4ed97e07ea7fae9325401b1ea5a460968f9da.svg)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186060908 :tutorial/content "To add or subtract vectors given in angle bracket or column vector form, we just need to add or subtract each component separately.

For example, in angle bracket notation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨2,5⟩+⟨-3,7⟩ & = \\ ⟨2+(-3),5+7⟩ & = \\ ⟨-1,12⟩ & ,\end{aligned}
$$

and in column vector notation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 7\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2+(-3) \\ 5+7\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 12\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Likewise, to multiply a vector given in angle bracket or column vector form, we just need to multiply each component separately.

For example, in angle bracket notation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-5\cdot ⟨2,5⟩ & = \\ ⟨(-5)\cdot 2,(-5)\cdot 5⟩ & = \\ ⟨-10,-25⟩ & ,\end{aligned}
$$

and in column vector notation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-5\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 5\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}(-5)\cdot 2 \\ (-5)\cdot 5\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-10 \\ -25\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186060909 :tutorial/content "To denote a vector, we have used two notations:

- a single bold lowercase letter, such as $\mathbf{v},$ or

- two uppercase letters representing the points of the ends of the vector, with an arrow over them, such as $\overrightarrow{AB}.$

We will mostly stick to these notations. However, there are many possible notations for vectors. For example, sometimes a vector can be denoted as

$$
\vec{v}, \quad \overrightarrow{V}, \quad v, \quad \hat{v}.
$$

The rightmost notation, $\hat{v},$ is usually used to represent unit vectors in particular." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186059922 :activity/expected-seconds 540.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054746 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-070008c9-e913-5456-a5af-e255c5aba081" "question-2e637b5f-6f34-5a1c-b2e1-f9ed9e9b050b"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-070008c9-e913-5456-a5af-e255c5aba081" :question/id #uuid "070008c9-e913-5456-a5af-e255c5aba081" :question/math-academy-id "q-30824" :question/problem "${log}_{64}⁡(\sqrt{8})=$" :question/worked-solution "We use the change of base formula:

$$
{log}_{a}⁡X=\frac{{log}_{b}⁡X}{{log}_{b}⁡a}
$$

In our case, $a=64$ and $X=\sqrt{8}.$ Since both $a$ and $X$ can be presented as a power of $8,$ we set $b=8.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{64}⁡(\sqrt{8}) & =\frac{{log}_{8}⁡(\sqrt{8})}{{log}_{8}⁡(64)} \\  & =\frac{{log}_{8}⁡({8}^{1/2})}{{log}_{8}⁡({8}^{2})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{1}{2})}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-cd14762e-d61e-513a-9786-dfc287bdc4a2"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-cd14762e-d61e-513a-9786-dfc287bdc4a2" :answer-field/id #uuid "cd14762e-d61e-513a-9786-dfc287bdc4a2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-38a98641-2e38-578c-b3c5-17bb1f192700" :answer-field/choices ["answer-5e7dce6a-3e36-598d-9a5e-9b0c2908e50b" "answer-9d4fd407-f836-5227-93e6-01c0887c14a9" "answer-e1e77c3b-5d54-5798-8bc6-98d8b4b1e688" "answer-38a98641-2e38-578c-b3c5-17bb1f192700" "answer-9b66ccb7-9147-50dc-a184-c4ff564b8209"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5e7dce6a-3e36-598d-9a5e-9b0c2908e50b" :answer/id #uuid "5e7dce6a-3e36-598d-9a5e-9b0c2908e50b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9d4fd407-f836-5227-93e6-01c0887c14a9" :answer/id #uuid "9d4fd407-f836-5227-93e6-01c0887c14a9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e1e77c3b-5d54-5798-8bc6-98d8b4b1e688" :answer/id #uuid "e1e77c3b-5d54-5798-8bc6-98d8b4b1e688" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-38a98641-2e38-578c-b3c5-17bb1f192700" :answer/id #uuid "38a98641-2e38-578c-b3c5-17bb1f192700" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9b66ccb7-9147-50dc-a184-c4ff564b8209" :answer/id #uuid "9b66ccb7-9147-50dc-a184-c4ff564b8209" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{8}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-2e637b5f-6f34-5a1c-b2e1-f9ed9e9b050b" :question/id #uuid "2e637b5f-6f34-5a1c-b2e1-f9ed9e9b050b" :question/math-academy-id "q-66885" :question/problem "${log}_{64}⁡(\sqrt[3]{4})=$" :question/worked-solution "We use the change of base formula:

$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to convert $P$ to row echelon form:

$$

Let $A(-2,0)$ and $B(3,3).$ Find $|\overset{\to }{AB}|.$ Do not round the answer.

$|\overset{\to }{AB}|=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We have 

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{OA}=a=-2i+0j, \\  & \overset{\to }{OB}=b=3i+3j.\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing $\overset{\to }{AB}$ as the difference of position vectors, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =\overset{\to }{OB}-\overset{\to }{OA} \\  & =b-a \\  & =(3i+3j)-(-2i+0j) \\  & =5i+3j.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the formula for the magnitude of a vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|\overset{\to }{AB}| & =\sqrt{{5}^{2}+{3}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25+9} \\  & =\sqrt{34}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f71eec51-55f5-5ed3-a5a6-c93f3bce746d"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-f71eec51-55f5-5ed3-a5a6-c93f3bce746d" :answer-field/id #uuid "f71eec51-55f5-5ed3-a5a6-c93f3bce746d" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-200a4d21-812f-5dd9-a1e8-34e8c33d93df" :answer-field/choices ["answer-200a4d21-812f-5dd9-a1e8-34e8c33d93df"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-200a4d21-812f-5dd9-a1e8-34e8c33d93df" :answer/id #uuid "200a4d21-812f-5dd9-a1e8-34e8c33d93df" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\sqrt{34}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-8c1db841-92ab-5a9b-b59a-bd03ce09afe3" :question/id #uuid "8c1db841-92ab-5a9b-b59a-bd03ce09afe3" :question/math-academy-id "q-18057" :question/problem "![](images/b9/b911126b4468e016afbab7faaf20223d0811827bb7f57cdefc2f1923cb7faf1b.png)

Points $A$ and $C$ are shown in the picture above. Find $|\overset{\to }{AC}|.$" :question/worked-solution "From the picture, we obtain $A(0,3)$ and $C(4,0).$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{OA}=a=0i+3j, \\  & \overset{\to }{OC}=c=4i+0j.\end{aligned}

Expressing $\overset{\to }{AC}$ as the difference of position vectors, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AC} & =\overset{\to }{OC}-\overset{\to }{OA} \\  & =c-a \\  & =(4i)-(3j) \\  & =4i-3j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the formula for the magnitude of a vector, we get

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We have 

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{OA}=a=0i+3j, \\  & \overset{\to }{OB}=b=4i-j.\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing $\overset{\to }{AB}$ as the difference of position vectors, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =\overset{\to }{OB}-\overset{\to }{OA} \\  & =b-a \\  & =(4i-j)-(0i+3j) \\  & =4i-4j.\end{aligned}

Now, using the formula for the magnitude of a vector, we get

$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-19605a89-6fbc-50e5-80b4-4cc3c9941a36"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-19605a89-6fbc-50e5-80b4-4cc3c9941a36" :answer-field/id #uuid "19605a89-6fbc-50e5-80b4-4cc3c9941a36" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-7001357a-d27f-5f38-bb51-c1671b2f85e3" :answer-field/choices ["answer-7001357a-d27f-5f38-bb51-c1671b2f85e3"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7001357a-d27f-5f38-bb51-c1671b2f85e3" :answer/id #uuid "7001357a-d27f-5f38-bb51-c1671b2f85e3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4\sqrt{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186059716 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-54931a2c-0179-55ba-b42e-021e69939399" "question-efcda90e-97e9-5de4-ab6e-f342fb013418"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-54931a2c-0179-55ba-b42e-021e69939399" :question/id #uuid "54931a2c-0179-55ba-b42e-021e69939399" :question/math-academy-id "q-70415" :question/problem "Let $r=\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ and $s=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}.$ Find a unit vector that is parallel to $3r+2s$ and points the same direction." :question/worked-solution "Remember that to find a unit vector that is parallel to a given vector and points the same direction., we need to divide the given vector by its length:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =\frac{3r+2s}{|3r+2s|}\end{aligned}
$$

First, let's compute the sum:

$$
\begin{aligned}3r+2s & =3\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+2\cdot \begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}(-6)+0 \\ 3+(-6)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula for the magnitude of a vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|3r+2s| & =\sqrt{(-6)^{2}+(-3)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{45} \\  & =3\sqrt{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide $3r+2s$ by its length and get the following unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =\frac{3r+2s}{|3r+2s|} \\  & =\frac{1}{3\sqrt{5}}(3r+2s) \\  & =\frac{1}{3\sqrt{5}}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-6 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-486b8f01-6945-5809-91a8-88d9d6a85f09"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $r$ and points the same direction." :question/worked-solution "Remember that to find a unit vector that is parallel to a given vector and points the same direction, we need to divide the given vector by its length:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =\frac{r}{|\,r\,|}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula for the magnitude of a vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|\,r\,| & =\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+(-6)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9+36} \\  & =\sqrt{45} \\  & =3\sqrt{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide $r$ by its length and get the following unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =\frac{r}{|r|} \\  & =\frac{1}{3\sqrt{5}}\cdot r \\  & =\frac{1}{3\sqrt{5}}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ -6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-ad9dfc42-a7b2-570f-831f-bdb8b850c4c5"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $\mathbf{a}=\langle -2,4 \rangle$ shown below.

![](images/cd/cd458eeb41ee09d6a4f58bc343575d46e3d362dc3edca40a47e1a7381fcc9bd2.png)

Expressed in component form, our vector is $\mathbf{a}=-2\mathbf{i} + 4 \mathbf{j}.$

To find the magnitude (length) of $\mathbf{a},$ we can use the Pythagorean theorem on $\triangle OXA.$

The legs of the triangle have lengths

$$
\begin{aligned}|\overset{\to }{OX}| & =|-2|=2\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}|\overset{\to }{XA}| & =|\,4\,|=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the Pythagorean theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\,a\,| & =\sqrt{|\overset{\to }{OX}{|}^{2}+|\overset{\to }{XA}{|}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{5}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186060911 :tutorial/content "We just saw that the magnitude of the vector $\mathbf{a}=\langle -2,4 \rangle$ was given by

$$
\begin{aligned}|\,a\,| & =\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

In general, given a vector
![](images/10/10fbddb6dc3528629e5583ad25976d049ca2ec5943ce3e689953f79299b8afcd.svg)
the magnitude of the vector can always be computed as

$$
|\,\mathbf{a}\,| = \sqrt{a_x^2+a_y^2}.
$$

**Note**

We sometimes use the notation $|| \mathbf a ||$ to denote the magnitude of a vector." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186059899 :activity/expected-seconds 540.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186059777 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-ec004b06-3312-5bf4-be49-682afc34bcbf" "question-c2988660-d9f8-5b55-910c-35b17be03f50"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-ec004b06-3312-5bf4-be49-682afc34bcbf" :question/id #uuid "ec004b06-3312-5bf4-be49-682afc34bcbf" :question/math-academy-id "q-182531" :question/problem "If $A$ is false and $B$ is true, then $A⇔B$ is

- $A⇔B$ is true if $A⇒B$ **and** $B⇒A.$ Otherwise, it is false.

- In other words, $A⇔B$ is true if $A$ and $B$ have the same truth values. Otherwise, it is false.

$$
\begin{aligned}(A⇔B) & =(\text{F}⇔\text{T}) \\  & =\text{F}.\end{aligned}
$$

| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |

"First, we use the definition of the biconditional statement to write the equivalence as a conjunction of implications: 

$$
¬(R⇔¬S)≡¬[(R⇒¬S)∧(¬S⇒R)]
$$

Now, we represent all the implications using disjunctions and negations:

$$
¬[(R⇒¬S)∧(¬S⇒R)]≡¬[(¬R∨¬S)∧(¬¬S∨R)]
$$

Next, we simplify the double negations:

$$
¬[(¬R∨¬S)∧(¬¬S∨R)]≡¬[(¬R∨¬S)∧(S∨R)]
$$

Now, we use De Morgan's laws:

$$
\begin{aligned}¬[(¬R∨¬S)∧(S∨R)] & ≡¬(¬R∨¬S)∨¬(S∨R) \\  & ≡(¬¬R∧¬¬S)∨¬(S∨R)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we again simplify the double negations and write down symbols in alphabetic order inside the parentheses using commutative laws:

$$
\begin{aligned}(¬¬R∧¬¬S)∨¬(S∨R) & ≡(R∧S)∨¬(S∨R) \\  & ≡(R∧S)∨¬(R∨S)\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a7422327-ad06-592f-a13d-35e60fbb5a20"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$

$$

Which statement is logically equivalent to the conditional statement above?"] ["question-cf7bb594-de49-54f5-b420-2e5186a68020" :question/worked-solution "Let's denote by $A$ and $B$ the following statements:

- $A:$ You don't turn the volume up.

- $B:$ You won't hear what they're saying.

Then, our initial statement can be written as $A⇒B,$ which is logically equivalent to 

$$
¬A∨B.

From the graph, we see that the line intercepts the $y$-axis at $(0,3).$ So, the $y$-intercept is $b=3.$

We can calculate the slope of the line by choosing two points on the line and applying the slope formula. The line passes through the points $(0,3)$ and $(-2,-1),$ so we calculate its slope as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}} \\  & =\frac{-1-3}{-2-0} \\  & =\frac{-4}{-2} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the slope $m=2$ and the $y$-intercept $b=3$ into the slope-intercept form $y=mx+b,$ we obtain the equation of the line:

$$
y=2x+3
$$"] ["question-5a315de4-d76f-5902-ac75-57586afb2f01" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-bd5cb081-453f-5660-95d6-9625673b4cec" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

$$
\begin{aligned}12z+7 & \le -5 &  &  & 12z+7 & \ge 5 \\ 12z & \le -12 &  &  & 12z & \ge -2 \\ z & \le -1 &  &  & z & \ge -\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem "What is the solution to the following system of inequalities?

\{\begin{aligned}p-2>3 \\ 1-2p\le -7\end{aligned}

- First, we solve $p-2>3\,:$

$$
\begin{aligned}p-2 & >3 \\ p-2+2 & >3+2 \\ p & >5\end{aligned}
$$

$$

- Then, we solve $1-2p\le -7\,:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}1-2p & \le -7 \\ 1-2p-1 & \le -7-1 \\ -2p & \le -8 \\ (-1)\cdot (-2p) & \ge (-1)\cdot (-8) \\ 2p & \ge 8 \\ \frac{2p}{2} & \ge \frac{8}{2} \\ p & \ge 4\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/f8/f8bf3ae94c8048dcf9060c985300f9a808ae73158eeeef6e0f01f3f922d33ea9.png)

:question/problem "What is $0.9\,\text{g}$ expressed in $\text{mg}?$ Write your answer as a whole number.

$0.9\,\text{g}=$
{{field-1}}$\text{mg}$"] ["question-fa1ab2c6-2c4e-5cd2-a497-7648fbd76dfd" :question/worked-solution "We start by recalling the conversion table for mass units. 

| Name | Symbol | Conversion |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kilogram | $\text{kg}$ | $1\,\text{kg}=1\,000\,\text{g}$ |
| Gram | $\text{g}$ | Base Unit |
| Milligram | $\text{mg}$ | $1\,000\,\text{mg}=1\,\text{g}$ |

$$

$$

There are $1\,000\,\text{mg}$ per $\text{g},$ which we can write as follows:

$$
\frac{1000\,\text{mg}}{\text{g}}
$$

This is our conversion factor.

Now, multiplying $0.9\,\text{g}$ by our conversion factor, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}0.9\,\text{g} & =0.9\,\text{g}\cdot \frac{1\,000\,\text{mg}}{\text{g}} \\  & =0.9\,\cancel{\text{g}}\cdot \frac{1\,000\,\text{mg}}{\cancel{\text{g}}} \\  & =0.9\cdot 1\,000\,\text{mg} \\  & =900\,\text{mg}.\end{aligned}
$$

["question-5021d5eb-c519-52ae-b30c-1049345fdc26" :question/problem "A triangle has sides $m$, $n$, and $o.$ The sides $m$, $n$, and $o$ are of lengths  $2$, $5$, and $6$, respectively. What is the measure of the angle between the sides $n$ and $o?$ Round your answer to two decimal places."] ["question-5021d5eb-c519-52ae-b30c-1049345fdc26" :question/worked-solution "The following triangle illustrates the information given.

![](images/26/26f2041aec84bb0086e2f08c2ba3a19331895951782b7fda153858643a8a5dd4.png)

We use the Law of Cosines to solve for angle $M:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡M & =\frac{{o}^{2}+{n}^{2}-{m}^{2}}{2no}.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Here, we have

$$
m=2,\,n=5,\,o=6.
$$

This gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡M & =\frac{{6}^{2}+{5}^{2}-{2}^{2}}{2(5)(6)} \\  & =\frac{36+25-4}{60} \\  & =\frac{57}{60}.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠M & =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{57}{60}) \\  & ={18.19}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to two decimal places."] ["question-5021d5eb-c519-52ae-b30c-1049345fdc26" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-fe46b4b1-2f2f-5fb3-9e1d-afbfc19fa446"
