["question-edd7453d-0827-54b9-87f7-014fa66cf7ec" :question/math-academy-id "q-14506"] ["question-edd7453d-0827-54b9-87f7-014fa66cf7ec" :question/problem "A triangle has sides $j$, $k$, and $l.$ The sides $j$ and $l$ have lengths $4$ and $7$, respectively. If the angle $K$ between $j$ and $l$ has a measure of ${121}^{∘}$, what is the length of side $k?$ Round your answer to two decimal places."] ["question-edd7453d-0827-54b9-87f7-014fa66cf7ec" :question/worked-solution "The following triangle illustrates the information given.

![](images/1f/1fde3029f6a50388ebd342dc4d15e9787567461b651c24cd6bd6843521b0465d.png)

The Law of Cosines states that

$$
{k}^{2}={j}^{2}+{l}^{2}-2jl\operatorname{cos}⁡K.
$$

Here, we have

$$
m∠K={121}^{∘},\,j=4,\,l=7.
$$

Substituting the numbers into the formula gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{k}^{2} & ={4}^{2}+{7}^{2}-2(4)(7)\operatorname{cos}⁡{121}^{∘} \\  & =16+49-56\operatorname{cos}⁡{121}^{∘} \\  & =65-56(-0.515\,03…) \\  & =65+28.842\,13 \\  & =93.842\,13\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $5$ decimal places. 

Taking the square root gives

$$
k=\sqrt{93.842\,13}=9.69
$$

rounded to two decimal places."] ["question-edd7453d-0827-54b9-87f7-014fa66cf7ec" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-e61d7995-875b-5a12-bc2c-d4a1dc9575fb" -1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 \\ -2 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix},$ find $det(A).$"] ["question-40a39262-0d1b-5421-8009-5952de54d116" :question/worked-solution "Given two $n\times n$ matrices $M$ and $N,$ we have

$$
det(MN)=det(M)\cdot det(N).
$$

In our case, this gives

$$
det(A)=det\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot det\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 \\ -2 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

We can compute the required determinants as follows:

- For the first determinant, we can compute it using a Laplace expansion down the $2$nd column.

- For the second determinant, we can compute it using a Laplace expansion across the $3$rd row.

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}\cdot \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 \\ -2 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(-1)(-1)^{2+2}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix}\cdot 2(-1)^{3+3}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -2 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-(1-2)\cdot 2(1+2) \\  & =1\cdot 6 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-40a39262-0d1b-5421-8009-5952de54d116" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-24bab1b2-9f01-5a84-84a1-c134dbb4356a" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-59d8b4d6-365d-545b-a80d-dc97dcfbcac8" :question/math-academy-id "q-42997"] ["question-59d8b4d6-365d-545b-a80d-dc97dcfbcac8" :question/problem "Let $A,$ $B,$ and $C$ be square matrices. If $A=B\cdot C,$  $|B|=9$ and $|{C}^{-1}|=-3$, find $|A|.$"] ["question-59d8b4d6-365d-545b-a80d-dc97dcfbcac8" :question/worked-solution "Given two $n\times n$ matrices $M$ and $N,$ we have

$$
det(MN)=det(M)\cdot det(N).
$$

Also, given an invertible $n\times n$ matrix $M,$ we have

$$
det({M}^{-1})=\frac{1}{det(M)}.
$$

Since $|C|=\frac{1}{|{C}^{-1}|}$, we get $|C|=-\frac{1}{3}.$

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}|A| & =|B|\cdot |C| \\  & =9\cdot (-\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-59d8b4d6-365d-545b-a80d-dc97dcfbcac8" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-7f31fc24-9a16-583f-8c7d-7e52bda34673" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
\overset{\to }{OR}={r}_{x}i+{r}_{y}\,j.
$$

Here, the point $R$ has coordinates $(-4,5),$ so its position vector is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OR} & =(-4)\cdot i+5\cdot j \\  & =-4\,i+5\,j.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-8f6ad506-8ae9-5d30-a511-9a3173b92b8c" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-17341d17-b542-5bd7-8870-0b8622258187" :answer-field/id #uuid "question-f0302994-59bc-5fe6-beeb-f786801b16b0"] [17592186101946 :tutorial/content "We can use Cartesian coordinates to define vectors in the plane. For example, consider the diagram shown below.

![](images/b7/b7fad622207f396145e930cf74f7905104bf12fa394a9f2f4f5d7ce761cc8e36.png)

The point $A$ has coordinates $(2,3).$ We also have the point $O(0,0)$ that is called the **origin**. 

The vector $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf{a}$ is called the **position vector** of $A.$ A position vector always has its tail at the origin. 

Now let's define two special unit vectors $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j},$ where $|\, \mathbf{i} \,| = |\, \mathbf{j} \,| = 1,$ as follows:

- $\mathbf{i}$ is a horizontal unit vector that points to the right along the positive direction of the $x$-axis, while

- $\mathbf{j}$ is a vertical unit vector that points upwards along the positive direction of the $y$-axis.

These vectors are shown in the picture below. 

![](images/cb/cb5694945b6f76f14a4e66b854f5daa56f3e607bd5b24c4f361ed844dbf8ff7e.png)

We have 

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{OX}=2i, \\  & \overset{\to }{XA}=\overset{\to }{OY}=3j.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, from $\triangle OXA,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OA} & =\overset{\to }{OX}+\overset{\to }{XA} \\  & =2i+3j.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the point $A$ with coordinates $(2,3)$ has a position vector

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OA} & =2i+3j.\end{aligned}
$$

In general, if a point $A$ has coordinates $(a_x,a_y),$ then its position vector is given by

$$
\overrightarrow{OA} = \mathbf{a} = a_x\mathbf{i}+a_y\mathbf{j}.
$$"] [17592186101947 :tutorial/content "The $\mathbf{i,j}$ notation can sometimes be cumbersome. An alternative is to use **angle bracket** notation. For example, using angle bracket notation, the vector $2\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}$ can be expressed as

$$
2\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}=\langle 2,3 \rangle.
$$

Note that, using angle bracket notation, the special unit vectors can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}i &=1i+0j=⟨1,0⟩, \\ j &=0i+1j=⟨0,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We can also use **column vector** notation, which is similar to angle bracket notation but expresses the vector as a column rather than a row. For example, using column vector notation, the vector $2\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}$ can be expressed as

![](images/24/2419e5c69bef2cc15f00106e4bf83a17ab2277ed5ea43e8b17f904ca6318873f.svg)

Using column vector notation, the special unit vectors can be expressed as ![](images/f5/f51854ec5bb92b38e5078cfe96046535f8e8efecf1304ea5cc4605dddec09573.svg) and ![](images/ff/ff6013f4f80815a7ca97b5ba8929c2d39b2a4e0165cbb5a8534d8ffafc4377e8.svg)

**Note:** Sometimes, the round bracket notation $(\ldots)$ is used to denote vectors. However, we will avoid using that notation here, because it also looks like the coordinates of a point. A point and its position vector are two separate objects!"] [17592186101948 :tutorial/content "If $A$ and $B$ are points in the Cartesian plane with position vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ respectively, then

$$
\overrightarrow{AB} = \mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}.
$$

To understand why the equation above is true, remember that $\overrightarrow{OA} = \mathbf{a}$ and $\overrightarrow{OB} = \mathbf{b}.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =\overset{\to }{AO}+\overset{\to }{OB} \\  & =-\overset{\to }{OA}+\overset{\to }{OB} \\  & =-a+b \\  & =b-a.\end{aligned}
$$

For example, given $A(5,13)$ and $B(-2,-35)$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{OA}=a=5i+13j, \\  & \overset{\to }{OB}=b=-2i-35j.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =b-a \\  & =(-2i-35j)-(5i+13j) \\  & =-7i-48j.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186101032 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0] ["question-e56f348b-304a-594f-855c-44aa9e7abb11" :question/id #uuid "e56f348b-304a-594f-855c-44aa9e7abb11"] ["question-e56f348b-304a-594f-855c-44aa9e7abb11" :question/math-academy-id "q-16096"] ["question-e56f348b-304a-594f-855c-44aa9e7abb11" :question/problem "The values of functions $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ and their derivatives at $x=-4$ are given in the table below.

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =a{y}^{3}{e}^{x-1}+3{x}^{2}{e}^{y-1}, \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & ={x}^{3}{e}^{y-1}+3b{y}^{2}{e}^{x-1}, \\ {f}_{x}(1,1) & =4.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-71adc372-d2f3-5857-a2ad-a0dc4396f12a" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the mixed partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{x}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(a{y}^{3}{e}^{x-1}+3{x}^{2}{e}^{y-1}) \\  & =3a{y}^{2}{e}^{x-1}+3{x}^{2}{e}^{y-1} \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{y}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}{e}^{y-1}+3b{y}^{2}{e}^{x-1}) \\  & =3{x}^{2}{e}^{y-1}+3b{y}^{2}{e}^{x-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. Hence, we have the identity

$$
\begin{aligned}3a{y}^{2}{e}^{x-1}+3{x}^{2}{e}^{y-1} &=3{x}^{2}{e}^{y-1}+3b{y}^{2}{e}^{x-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of ${y}^{2}{e}^{x-1},$ respectively, we see that $a=b.$ 

Since ${f}_{x}(1,1)=4$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,1) & =4 \\ a(1)^{3}{e}^{0}+3(1)^{2}{e}^{0} & =4 \\ a+3 & =4 \\ a & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
b=a=1.

:question/problem "Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Find the values of $a$ and $b$, if 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =2ax{y}^{2}-4xy+15x, \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =b{x}^{2}y-2{x}^{2}-4y, \\ {f}_{y}(-1,-1) & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-fcbd8ac8-2f1b-5dcb-9ac1-2425c8503e58" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the mixed partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{x}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2ax{y}^{2}-4xy+15x) \\  & =4axy-4x-0 \\  & =4axy-4x \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{y}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(b{x}^{2}y-2{x}^{2}-4y) \\  & =2bxy-4x-0 \\  & =2bxy-4x\end{aligned}
$$

Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. Hence, we have the identity

$$
\begin{aligned}4axy-4x &=2bxy-4x.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $xy$, we see that $a=\frac{b}{2}.$ 

Now, since ${f}_{y}(-1,-1)=-5$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(-1,-1) & =-5 \\ b(-1)^{2}(-1)-2(-1)^{2}-4(-1) & =-5 \\ -b-2+4 & =-5 \\ b & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
a=\frac{b}{2}=\frac{7}{2}.
$$"] ["question-fcbd8ac8-2f1b-5dcb-9ac1-2425c8503e58" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-ff468151-5610-57e8-a342-0015e9de243b" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "Suppose that a function $f(x,y,z)$ and all of its higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ and that

$$
{f}_{zx}(x,y,z)=-\frac{2yz}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},\,{f}_{yz}(x,y,z)=\frac{2xz}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$

 

Evaluate the following expression at the point $(1,2,1):$

$$
{f}_{zyy}(x,y,z)+{f}_{xxz}(x,y,z)
$$"] ["question-0032ce9b-c24d-5a4a-8814-0479ffd35234" :question/worked-solution "As the higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. 

Hence, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{zyy}(x,y,z) & ={f}_{yzy}(x,y,z) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{yz}(x,y,z)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{2xz}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}) \\  & =-\frac{4xyz}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In addition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xxz}(x,y,z) & ={f}_{zxx}(x,y,z) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{zx}(x,y,z)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-\frac{2yz}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{4xyz}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the above, we get

$$
{f}_{zyy}(x,y,z)+{f}_{xxz}(x,y,z)=-\frac{4xyz}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})^{2}}+\frac{4xyz}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})^{2}}=0.
$$

Finally, 

$$
{f}_{zyy}(1,2,1)+{f}_{xxz}(1,2,1)=0.
$$"] ["question-0032ce9b-c24d-5a4a-8814-0479ffd35234" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-94c40397-9482-5a52-b940-12d808c2acb6" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-8db2f83d-f6c6-583a-9190-f65543a5bd2c" :question/math-academy-id "q-138836"] ["question-8db2f83d-f6c6-583a-9190-f65543a5bd2c" :question/problem "Consider the function $y=\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{({x}^{2}-2x-8)^{2}}.$ The derivative of this function is given by

$$
{y}^{′}=\frac{2{e}^{{x}^{2}}g(x)}{({x}^{2}-2x-8)^{3}}.
$$

Find the function $g(x).$"] ["question-8db2f83d-f6c6-583a-9190-f65543a5bd2c" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y=\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{({x}^{2}-2x-8)^{2}}.
$$

First, we find the natural logarithm of both sides and use the quotient and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{({x}^{2}-2x-8)^{2}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{{x}^{2}})-\operatorname{ln}⁡{({x}^{2}-2x-8)}^{2} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & ={x}^{2}-2\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-2x-8)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}-2\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-2x-8)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =2x-2\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{2}-2x-8}\cdot (2x-2) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =2x-\frac{4x-4}{{x}^{2}-2x-8}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(2x-\frac{4x-4}{{x}^{2}-2x-8})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{({x}^{2}-2x-8)^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{({x}^{2}-2x-8)^{2}}(2x-\frac{4x-4}{{x}^{2}-2x-8}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{({x}^{2}-2x-8)^{2}}(\frac{2x({x}^{2}-2x-8)-(4x-4)}{{x}^{2}-2x-8}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{({x}^{2}-2x-8)^{3}}(2x({x}^{2}-2x-8)-(4x-4)) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{({x}^{2}-2x-8)^{3}}(2{x}^{3}-4{x}^{2}-16x-4x+4) \\  & =\frac{2{e}^{{x}^{2}}({x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}-10x+2)}{({x}^{2}-2x-8)^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
g(x)={x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}-10x+2.
$$"] ["question-8db2f83d-f6c6-583a-9190-f65543a5bd2c" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-0e4c95de-4b57-5003-8261-a6e1c6a6bcc0" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "Evaluate the following limit:

${lim}_{n\to 0}{(1+n)}^{4/7n}=$
{{field-1}}"] ["question-0ac40a4c-aba2-5c77-8ace-67895a16cfed" :question/worked-solution "Notice that as $n\to 0,$ 

- the expression inside the parentheses approaches $1,$ while

- the exponent approaches $\infty .$

So, if we attempt to evaluate the limit directly, we get

$$
{lim}_{n\to 0}{(1+n)}^{4/7n}={1}^{\infty },
$$

which is an indeterminate form.

Instead, let's recall the following special limit:

$$
{lim}_{n\to 0}{(1+n)}^{1/n}=e
$$

Rewriting the given limit using the algebra of limits and applying our special limit, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{n\to 0}{(1+n)}^{4/7n} & ={lim}_{n\to 0}{[{(1+n)}^{1/n}]}^{4/7} \\  & ={[{lim}_{n\to 0}{(1+n)}^{1/n}]}^{4/7} \\  & ={e}^{4/7} \\  & =\sqrt[7]{{e}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-0ac40a4c-aba2-5c77-8ace-67895a16cfed" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-7e129902-6deb-5f56-af1c-12c6f695aaf0" :answer-field/id #uuid "7e129902-6deb-5f56-af1c-12c6f695aaf0"] ["answer-cb4fd080-504f-597c-84bf-48ecf4885982" :answer/id #uuid "cb4fd080-504f-597c-84bf-48ecf4885982"] ["answer-cb4fd080-504f-597c-84bf-48ecf4885982" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-cb4fd080-504f-597c-84bf-48ecf4885982" :answer/value "e^{\frac{4}{7}}"] ["answer-field-7e129902-6deb-5f56-af1c-12c6f695aaf0" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-7e129902-6deb-5f56-af1c-12c6f695aaf0" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-7e129902-6deb-5f56-af1c-12c6f695aaf0" :answer-field/correct "answer-cb4fd080-504f-597c-84bf-48ecf4885982"] ["answer-field-7e129902-6deb-5f56-af1c-12c6f695aaf0" :answer-field/choices "answer-cb4fd080-504f-597c-84bf-48ecf4885982"] ["question-0ac40a4c-aba2-5c77-8ace-67895a16cfed" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-7e129902-6deb-5f56-af1c-12c6f695aaf0"] [17592186176018 :knowledge-point/questions "question-0ac40a4c-aba2-5c77-8ace-67895a16cfed"] ["question-8f2aebee-176b-5447-94e6-cdb44a5559c2" :question/id #uuid "8f2aebee-176b-5447-94e6-cdb44a5559c2"] ["question-8f2aebee-176b-5447-94e6-cdb44a5559c2" :question/math-academy-id "q-351023"] ["question-8f2aebee-176b-5447-94e6-cdb44a5559c2" :question/problem "Evaluate the following integral. {{field-1}}"] ["question-8f2aebee-176b-5447-94e6-cdb44a5559c2" :question/worked-solution "First, we write the integral as

$$
{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})\,\text{d}x={\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}x.
$$

 

We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{3}{x} \\ {v}^{′}=1\, & ⟹\,v=\int 1\cdot \,dx=x\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}u{v}^{′}\text{d}x \\  & =uv{|}_{1}^{{e}^{2}}-{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}v{u}^{′}\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})\,(x){|}_{1}^{{e}^{2}}-{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}x(\frac{3}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =[\operatorname{ln}⁡(({e}^{2})^{3})\,({e}^{2})-\operatorname{ln}⁡({1}^{3})\,(1)]-3{\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{6})-3x{|}_{1}^{{e}^{2}} \\  & =6{e}^{2}-3({e}^{2}-1) \\  & =3({e}^{2}+1).\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-8f2aebee-176b-5447-94e6-cdb44a5559c2" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-8946e118-e7e3-5ee7-9e3c-9199dfb40a0e" :answer-field/id #uuid "8946e118-e7e3-5ee7-9e3c-9199dfb40a0e"] ["answer-4245b790-1a22-59f1-b2b1-ec25d43743c0" :answer/id #uuid "4245b790-1a22-59f1-b2b1-ec25d43743c0"] ["answer-4245b790-1a22-59f1-b2b1-ec25d43743c0" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-4245b790-1a22-59f1-b2b1-ec25d43743c0" :answer/value "3({e}^{2}+1)"] ["answer-field-8946e118-e7e3-5ee7-9e3c-9199dfb40a0e" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-8946e118-e7e3-5ee7-9e3c-9199dfb40a0e" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-8946e118-e7e3-5ee7-9e3c-9199dfb40a0e" :answer-field/correct "answer-4245b790-1a22-59f1-b2b1-ec25d43743c0"] ["answer-field-8946e118-e7e3-5ee7-9e3c-9199dfb40a0e" :answer-field/choices "answer-4245b790-1a22-59f1-b2b1-ec25d43743c0"] ["question-8f2aebee-176b-5447-94e6-cdb44a5559c2" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-8946e118-e7e3-5ee7-9e3c-9199dfb40a0e"] [17592186096836 :knowledge-point/questions "question-8f2aebee-176b-5447-94e6-cdb44a5559c2"] ["question-0c781737-7cc2-58de-b406-ca857cb292ed" :question/id #uuid "0c781737-7cc2-58de-b406-ca857cb292ed"] ["question-0c781737-7cc2-58de-b406-ca857cb292ed" :question/math-academy-id "q-339011"] ["question-0c781737-7cc2-58de-b406-ca857cb292ed" :question/problem "Find the value of $a$ given that

$$

$a=$
{{field-1}}"] ["question-0c781737-7cc2-58de-b406-ca857cb292ed" :question/worked-solution "First, we let 

$$
L=\frac{(\frac{1}{a+h}-\frac{1}{a})}{h}=-\frac{1}{4}.
$$

Comparing this with the formula for the instantaneous rate of change,

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h},
$$

we see that if we let $f(x)=\frac{1}{x}$, we get

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{(\frac{1}{a+h}-\frac{1}{a})}{h}=L.
$$

This confirms that $L={f}^{′}(a).$

Computing the derivative, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}},\,{f}^{′}(a)=-\frac{1}{{a}^{2}},
$$

and so,  $L=-\frac{1}{{a}^{2}}.$

Finally, since $L=-\frac{1}{4},$ we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{{a}^{2}} & =-\frac{1}{4} \\ {a}^{2} & =4 \\ a & =\pm 2.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-0c781737-7cc2-58de-b406-ca857cb292ed" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-566ccb36-6055-535a-bafd-ee2a268c69a1" :answer-field/id #uuid "question-d424dcb1-177c-5053-898f-bbc5de5cd766"] [17592186060907 :tutorial/content "Suppose we are given two vectors 
$\mathbf{a} = \langle 2,3 \rangle$ and $\mathbf{b} = \langle -4,4 \rangle,$ shown below. How do we compute the vectors $\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}$  and  $-5\mathbf{a}$ in terms of the standard basis $\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}?$

![](images/25/254809cbc834b493759a6fa09222a2c90c5fbfc3280d22e82470e760a7a4c508.png)

To compute $\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b},$ we collect all of the $\mathbf{i}$'s and $\mathbf{j}$'s. We know that $\mathbf{a} = {\color{red}2}\mathbf{i} + {\color{blue}3}\mathbf{j}$ and $\mathbf{b} = {\color{red}-4}\mathbf{i} + {\color{blue}4}\mathbf{j}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b & =(2i+3j)+(-4i+4j) \\  & =(2+(-4))i+(3+4)j \\  & =-2i+7j.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing our answer in angle bracket and column vector notations, we get 
![](images/ea/eae25a74dde73f7899f6ccbbdbb1a1f589fc72cad9629a33b4fdbbbc753efcd8.svg)

To compute $-5\mathbf{a},$ we multiply each of the components by $-5\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}-5\cdot a & =-5(2i+3j) \\  & =(-5\cdot 2)i+(-5\cdot 3)j \\  & =-10i+-15j\end{aligned}
$$

Writing our answer in angle bracket and column vector notations, we get 
![](images/05/05f847a73201db3de20db3847ef4ed97e07ea7fae9325401b1ea5a460968f9da.svg)"] [17592186060908 :tutorial/content "To add or subtract vectors given in angle bracket or column vector form, we just need to add or subtract each component separately.

For example, in angle bracket notation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨2,5⟩+⟨-3,7⟩ & = \\ ⟨2+(-3),5+7⟩ & = \\ ⟨-1,12⟩ & ,\end{aligned}
$$

and in column vector notation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 7\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2+(-3) \\ 5+7\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 12\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Likewise, to multiply a vector given in angle bracket or column vector form, we just need to multiply each component separately.

For example, in angle bracket notation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-5\cdot ⟨2,5⟩ & = \\ ⟨(-5)\cdot 2,(-5)\cdot 5⟩ & = \\ ⟨-10,-25⟩ & ,\end{aligned}
$$

and in column vector notation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-5\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 5\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}(-5)\cdot 2 \\ (-5)\cdot 5\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-10 \\ -25\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186060909 :tutorial/content "To denote a vector, we have used two notations:

- a single bold lowercase letter, such as $\mathbf{v},$ or

- two uppercase letters representing the points of the ends of the vector, with an arrow over them, such as $\overrightarrow{AB}.$

We will mostly stick to these notations. However, there are many possible notations for vectors. For example, sometimes a vector can be denoted as

$$
\vec{v}, \quad \overrightarrow{V}, \quad v, \quad \hat{v}.
$$

The rightmost notation, $\hat{v},$ is usually used to represent unit vectors in particular."] [17592186059922 :activity/expected-seconds 540.0] ["question-070008c9-e913-5456-a5af-e255c5aba081" :question/id #uuid "070008c9-e913-5456-a5af-e255c5aba081"] ["question-070008c9-e913-5456-a5af-e255c5aba081" :question/math-academy-id "q-30824"] ["question-070008c9-e913-5456-a5af-e255c5aba081" :question/problem "${log}_{64}⁡(\sqrt{8})=$"] ["question-070008c9-e913-5456-a5af-e255c5aba081" :question/worked-solution "We use the change of base formula:

$$
{log}_{a}⁡X=\frac{{log}_{b}⁡X}{{log}_{b}⁡a}
$$

In our case, $a=64$ and $X=\sqrt{8}.$ Since both $a$ and $X$ can be presented as a power of $8,$ we set $b=8.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{64}⁡(\sqrt{8}) & =\frac{{log}_{8}⁡(\sqrt{8})}{{log}_{8}⁡(64)} \\  & =\frac{{log}_{8}⁡({8}^{1/2})}{{log}_{8}⁡({8}^{2})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{1}{2})}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-070008c9-e913-5456-a5af-e255c5aba081" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-cd14762e-d61e-513a-9786-dfc287bdc4a2" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "${log}_{64}⁡(\sqrt[3]{4})=$"] ["question-2e637b5f-6f34-5a1c-b2e1-f9ed9e9b050b" :question/worked-solution "We use the change of base formula:

$$
{log}_{a}⁡X=\frac{{log}_{b}⁡X}{{log}_{b}⁡a}
$$

In our case, $a=64$ and $X=\sqrt[3]{4}.$ Since both $a$ and $X$ can be presented as a power of $4,$ we set $b=4.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{64}⁡(\sqrt[3]{4}) & =\frac{{log}_{4}⁡(\sqrt[3]{4})}{{log}_{4}⁡(64)} \\  & =\frac{{log}_{4}⁡({4}^{1/3})}{{log}_{4}⁡({4}^{3})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{1}{3})}{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-2e637b5f-6f34-5a1c-b2e1-f9ed9e9b050b" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-b211c988-c894-53a3-abe3-c7c0de871b39" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

Let $A(-2,0)$ and $B(3,3).$ Find $|\overset{\to }{AB}|.$ Do not round the answer.

$|\overset{\to }{AB}|=$
{{field-1}}"] ["question-a88ebacd-81cc-571b-8835-0aed7b200fdc" :question/worked-solution "We have 

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{OA}=a=-2i+0j, \\  & \overset{\to }{OB}=b=3i+3j.\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing $\overset{\to }{AB}$ as the difference of position vectors, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =\overset{\to }{OB}-\overset{\to }{OA} \\  & =b-a \\  & =(3i+3j)-(-2i+0j) \\  & =5i+3j.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the formula for the magnitude of a vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|\overset{\to }{AB}| & =\sqrt{{5}^{2}+{3}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25+9} \\  & =\sqrt{34}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-a88ebacd-81cc-571b-8835-0aed7b200fdc" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-f71eec51-55f5-5ed3-a5a6-c93f3bce746d" :answer-field/id #uuid "f71eec51-55f5-5ed3-a5a6-c93f3bce746d"] ["answer-200a4d21-812f-5dd9-a1e8-34e8c33d93df" :answer/id #uuid "200a4d21-812f-5dd9-a1e8-34e8c33d93df"] ["answer-200a4d21-812f-5dd9-a1e8-34e8c33d93df" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-200a4d21-812f-5dd9-a1e8-34e8c33d93df" :answer/value "\sqrt{34}"] ["answer-field-f71eec51-55f5-5ed3-a5a6-c93f3bce746d" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-f71eec51-55f5-5ed3-a5a6-c93f3bce746d" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-f71eec51-55f5-5ed3-a5a6-c93f3bce746d" :answer-field/correct "answer-200a4d21-812f-5dd9-a1e8-34e8c33d93df"] ["answer-field-f71eec51-55f5-5ed3-a5a6-c93f3bce746d" :answer-field/choices "answer-200a4d21-812f-5dd9-a1e8-34e8c33d93df"] ["question-a88ebacd-81cc-571b-8835-0aed7b200fdc" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-f71eec51-55f5-5ed3-a5a6-c93f3bce746d"] [17592186059715 :knowledge-point/questions "question-a88ebacd-81cc-571b-8835-0aed7b200fdc"] ["question-8c1db841-92ab-5a9b-b59a-bd03ce09afe3" :question/id #uuid "8c1db841-92ab-5a9b-b59a-bd03ce09afe3"] ["question-8c1db841-92ab-5a9b-b59a-bd03ce09afe3" :question/math-academy-id "q-18057"] ["question-8c1db841-92ab-5a9b-b59a-bd03ce09afe3" :question/problem "![](images/b9/b911126b4468e016afbab7faaf20223d0811827bb7f57cdefc2f1923cb7faf1b.png)

"![](images/45/453e8fc1c4d8a5262fd0a8aa7341dd71b909a4a72cec94cd2698f800f7dc06c9.png)

Let $A(0,3)$ and $B(4,-1).$ Find $|\overset{\to }{AB}|.$ Do not round the answer.

$|\overset{\to }{AB}|=$
{{field-1}}"] ["question-65c77d8f-4e68-5667-bebf-382cd66bf3e2" :question/worked-solution "We have 

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{OA}=a=0i+3j, \\  & \overset{\to }{OB}=b=4i-j.\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing $\overset{\to }{AB}$ as the difference of position vectors, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =\overset{\to }{OB}-\overset{\to }{OA} \\  & =b-a \\  & =(4i-j)-(0i+3j) \\  & =4i-4j.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the formula for the magnitude of a vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|\overset{\to }{AB}| & =\sqrt{{4}^{2}+(-4)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16+16} \\  & =4\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-65c77d8f-4e68-5667-bebf-382cd66bf3e2" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-19605a89-6fbc-50e5-80b4-4cc3c9941a36" :answer-field/id #uuid "19605a89-6fbc-50e5-80b4-4cc3c9941a36"] ["answer-7001357a-d27f-5f38-bb51-c1671b2f85e3" :answer/id #uuid "7001357a-d27f-5f38-bb51-c1671b2f85e3"] ["answer-7001357a-d27f-5f38-bb51-c1671b2f85e3" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-7001357a-d27f-5f38-bb51-c1671b2f85e3" :answer/value "4\sqrt{2}"] ["answer-field-19605a89-6fbc-50e5-80b4-4cc3c9941a36" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-19605a89-6fbc-50e5-80b4-4cc3c9941a36" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-19605a89-6fbc-50e5-80b4-4cc3c9941a36" :answer-field/correct "answer-7001357a-d27f-5f38-bb51-c1671b2f85e3"] ["answer-field-19605a89-6fbc-50e5-80b4-4cc3c9941a36" :answer-field/choices "answer-7001357a-d27f-5f38-bb51-c1671b2f85e3"] ["question-65c77d8f-4e68-5667-bebf-382cd66bf3e2" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-19605a89-6fbc-50e5-80b4-4cc3c9941a36"] [17592186059715 :knowledge-point/questions "question-65c77d8f-4e68-5667-bebf-382cd66bf3e2"] ["question-54931a2c-0179-55ba-b42e-021e69939399" :question/id #uuid "54931a2c-0179-55ba-b42e-021e69939399"] ["question-54931a2c-0179-55ba-b42e-021e69939399" :question/math-academy-id "q-70415"] ["question-54931a2c-0179-55ba-b42e-021e69939399" :question/problem "Let $r=\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ and $s=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}.$ Find a unit vector that is parallel to $3r+2s$ and points the same direction."] ["question-54931a2c-0179-55ba-b42e-021e69939399" :question/worked-solution "Remember that to find a unit vector that is parallel to a given vector and points the same direction., we need to divide the given vector by its length:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =\frac{3r+2s}{|3r+2s|}\end{aligned}
$$

First, let's compute the sum:

$$
\begin{aligned}3r+2s & =3\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+2\cdot \begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}(-6)+0 \\ 3+(-6)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-6 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula for the magnitude of a vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|3r+2s| & =\sqrt{(-6)^{2}+(-3)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{45} \\  & =3\sqrt{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide $3r+2s$ by its length and get the following unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =\frac{3r+2s}{|3r+2s|} \\  & =\frac{1}{3\sqrt{5}}(3r+2s) \\  & =\frac{1}{3\sqrt{5}}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-6 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-54931a2c-0179-55ba-b42e-021e69939399" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-486b8f01-6945-5809-91a8-88d9d6a85f09" :answer-field/id #uuid "question-efcda90e-97e9-5de4-ab6e-f342fb013418"] [17592186060910 :tutorial/content "Consider the vector $\mathbf{a}=\langle -2,4 \rangle$ shown below.

![](images/cd/cd458eeb41ee09d6a4f58bc343575d46e3d362dc3edca40a47e1a7381fcc9bd2.png)

Expressed in component form, our vector is $\mathbf{a}=-2\mathbf{i} + 4 \mathbf{j}.$

To find the magnitude (length) of $\mathbf{a},$ we can use the Pythagorean theorem on $\triangle OXA.$

The legs of the triangle have lengths

$$
\begin{aligned}|\overset{\to }{OX}| & =|-2|=2\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}|\overset{\to }{XA}| & =|\,4\,|=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the Pythagorean theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\,a\,| & =\sqrt{|\overset{\to }{OX}{|}^{2}+|\overset{\to }{XA}{|}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{5}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186060911 :tutorial/content "We just saw that the magnitude of the vector $\mathbf{a}=\langle -2,4 \rangle$ was given by

$$
\begin{aligned}|\,a\,| & =\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

In general, given a vector
![](images/10/10fbddb6dc3528629e5583ad25976d049ca2ec5943ce3e689953f79299b8afcd.svg)
the magnitude of the vector can always be computed as

$$
|\,\mathbf{a}\,| = \sqrt{a_x^2+a_y^2}.
$$

**Note**

We sometimes use the notation $|| \mathbf a ||$ to denote the magnitude of a vector."] [17592186059899 :activity/expected-seconds 540.0] ["question-ec004b06-3312-5bf4-be49-682afc34bcbf" :question/id #uuid "ec004b06-3312-5bf4-be49-682afc34bcbf"] ["question-ec004b06-3312-5bf4-be49-682afc34bcbf" :question/math-academy-id "q-182531"] ["question-ec004b06-3312-5bf4-be49-682afc34bcbf" :question/problem "If $A$ is false and $B$ is true, then $A⇔B$ is

{{field-1}}."] ["question-ec004b06-3312-5bf4-be49-682afc34bcbf" :question/worked-solution "According to the definition of the biconditional, 

- $A⇔B$ is true if $A⇒B$ **and** $B⇒A.$ Otherwise, it is false.

- In other words, $A⇔B$ is true if $A$ and $B$ have the same truth values. Otherwise, it is false.

So, when $A=\text{F}$ and $B=\text{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(A⇔B) & =(\text{F}⇔\text{T}) \\  & =\text{F}.\end{aligned}
$$

The complete truth table is shown below:

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,A⇔B\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |
|  |  |  |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ |

["question-babcf679-477c-52f6-b009-8d35e055441b" :question/worked-solution "First, we use the definition of the biconditional statement to write the equivalence as a conjunction of implications: 

$$
¬(R⇔¬S)≡¬[(R⇒¬S)∧(¬S⇒R)]
$$

Now, we represent all the implications using disjunctions and negations:

$$
¬[(R⇒¬S)∧(¬S⇒R)]≡¬[(¬R∨¬S)∧(¬¬S∨R)]
$$

Next, we simplify the double negations:

$$
¬[(¬R∨¬S)∧(¬¬S∨R)]≡¬[(¬R∨¬S)∧(S∨R)]
$$

Now, we use De Morgan's laws:

$$
\begin{aligned}¬[(¬R∨¬S)∧(S∨R)] & ≡¬(¬R∨¬S)∨¬(S∨R) \\  & ≡(¬¬R∧¬¬S)∨¬(S∨R)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we again simplify the double negations and write down symbols in alphabetic order inside the parentheses using commutative laws:

$$
\begin{aligned}(¬¬R∧¬¬S)∨¬(S∨R) & ≡(R∧S)∨¬(S∨R) \\  & ≡(R∧S)∨¬(R∨S)\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-babcf679-477c-52f6-b009-8d35e055441b" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-a7422327-ad06-592f-a13d-35e60fbb5a20" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "$¬(B⇔A)≡$"] ["question-f686088d-e105-5e19-956f-e84bb86ba487" :question/worked-solution "First, we use the definition of the biconditional statement to write the equivalence as a conjunction of implications: 

$$
¬(B⇔A)≡¬[(B⇒A)∧(A⇒B)]
$$

Now, we represent all the implications using disjunctions and negations:

$$
¬[(B⇒A)∧(A⇒B)]≡¬[(¬B∨A)∧(¬A∨B)]
$$

Next, we use De Morgan's laws:

$$
\begin{aligned}¬[(¬B∨A)∧(¬A∨B)] & ≡¬(¬B∨A)∨¬(¬A∨B) \\  & ≡(¬¬B∧¬A)∨(¬¬A∧¬B)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we simplify the double negations and write down symbols in alphabetic order inside the parentheses using commutative laws:

$$
\begin{aligned}(¬¬B∧¬A)∨(¬¬A∧¬B) & ≡(B∧¬A)∨(A∧¬B) \\  & ≡(¬A∧B)∨(A∧¬B)\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-f686088d-e105-5e19-956f-e84bb86ba487" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-4965da56-6033-5b41-a06c-91a9fdf4486b" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-0c4fe725-e7cf-5733-870d-da1a638a1a59" :question/math-academy-id "q-31944"] ["question-0c4fe725-e7cf-5733-870d-da1a638a1a59" :question/problem "The inverse of the $2\times 2$ matrix $P$ is found using row operations, as shown below. Complete the process, and determine ${P}^{-1}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}[P\,|\,I] & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :=-\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -\frac{1}{3} & -\frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -\frac{1}{3} & -\frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{5}{3} & \frac{2}{3} & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{3}{5}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -\frac{1}{3} & -\frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{2}{5} & \frac{3}{5}\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :=\text{___________} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{\phantom{a}} & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{\phantom{a}} \\ 0 & 1 & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{\phantom{a}} & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{\phantom{a}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-0c4fe725-e7cf-5733-870d-da1a638a1a59" :question/worked-solution "We write down $P$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply the standard Gauss-Jordan method to transform the matrix $P$ into the identity matrix. We perform the same row operations on both matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}[P\,|\,I] & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :=-\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -\frac{1}{3} & -\frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -\frac{1}{3} & -\frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{5}{3} & \frac{2}{3} & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{3}{5}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -\frac{1}{3} & -\frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{2}{5} & \frac{3}{5}\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & -\frac{1}{5} & \frac{1}{5} \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{2}{5} & \frac{3}{5}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The matrix ${P}^{-1}$ is given by the right-hand side of our big matrix after all of the transformations have been completed. Therefore, 

$$
{P}^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{5} & \frac{1}{5} \\ \frac{2}{5} & \frac{3}{5}\end{bmatrix}.
$$"] ["question-0c4fe725-e7cf-5733-870d-da1a638a1a59" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-8cea2ad4-e0cc-5ef8-b8e2-86f20e8d1d7a" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-fc1b75b6-fb85-5b50-9394-b22e6f324813" :question/math-academy-id "q-31950"] ["question-fc1b75b6-fb85-5b50-9394-b22e6f324813" :question/problem "The inverse of the $2\times 2$ matrix $H$ is found using row operations, as shown below. Complete the process, and determine ${H}^{-1}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}[H\,|\,I] & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -5 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{5}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -5 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & \frac{1}{5}\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :=\text{___________} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{\phantom{a}} & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{\phantom{a}} \\ 0 & 1 & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{\phantom{a}} & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{\phantom{a}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-fc1b75b6-fb85-5b50-9394-b22e6f324813" :question/worked-solution "We write down $H$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply the standard Gauss-Jordan method to transform the matrix $H$ into the identity matrix. We perform the same row operations on both matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}[H\,|\,I] & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -5 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{5}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -5 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & \frac{1}{5}\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+5{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & \frac{1}{5}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The matrix ${H}^{-1}$ is given by the right-hand side of our big matrix after all of the transformations have been completed. Therefore, 

$$
{H}^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{5}\end{bmatrix}.
$$"] ["question-fc1b75b6-fb85-5b50-9394-b22e6f324813" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-c6403903-5168-5e04-a6e9-85eb37526148" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "The inverse of the matrix $B$ is found using row operations, as shown below. What are the row operations corresponding to each step?

$$
\begin{aligned}[B\,|\,I] & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} &  & \text{___________} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -\frac{1}{3}\end{bmatrix} &  & \text{___________} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 1 & -\frac{2}{3} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -\frac{1}{3}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-2b6dc055-10e0-54e5-be96-be9101fa62fe" :question/worked-solution "We write down $B$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply the standard Gauss-Jordan method to transform the matrix $B$ into the identity matrix. We perform the same row operations on both matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}[B\,|\,I] & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :=-\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -\frac{1}{3}\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 1 & -\frac{2}{3} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -\frac{1}{3}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding row operations are

$$
{R}_{2}:=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2},\,{R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+2{R}_{2}.
$$

The matrix ${B}^{-1}$ is given by the right-hand side of our big matrix after all of the transformations have been completed. Therefore, 

$$
{B}^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -\frac{2}{3} \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{3}\end{bmatrix}.
$$"] ["question-2b6dc055-10e0-54e5-be96-be9101fa62fe" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-2c47d228-518f-5f23-905f-048259f6ebd8" :answer-field/id #uuid can use Cartesian coordinates to define vectors in the plane. For example, consider the diagram shown below.

![](images/b7/b7fad622207f396145e930cf74f7905104bf12fa394a9f2f4f5d7ce761cc8e36.png)

The point $A$ has coordinates $(2,3)$. We also have the point $O(0,0)$ that is called the **origin**.

The vector

$$
\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf{a}
$$

is called the **position vector** of $A$. A position vector always has its tail at the origin.

Now let's define two special unit vectors $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$, where

$$
\begin{vmatrix}\, \mathbf{i} \, & = & \, \mathbf{j} \,\end{vmatrix} = 1
$$

as follows:

- $\mathbf{i}$ is a horizontal unit vector that points to the right along the positive direction of the $x$-axis, while
- $\mathbf{j}$ is a vertical unit vector that points upwards along the positive direction of the $y$-axis.

These vectors are shown in the picture below.

![](images/cb/cb5694945b6f76f14a4e66b854f5daa56f3e607bd5b24c4f361ed844dbf8ff7e.png)

We have

$$
OX^(→) = 2i,; XA^(→) = OY^(→) = 3j
$$

Now, from $\triangle OXA$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
OA^(→) &= OX^(→) + XA^(→) \\
&= 2i + 3j
\end{aligned}
$$

So, the point $A$ with coordinates $(2,3)$ has a position vector

$$
\begin{aligned}
OA^(→) &= 2i + 3j
\end{aligned}
$$

In general, if a point $A$ has coordinates $(a_x,a_y)$, then its position vector is given by

$$
\overrightarrow{OA} = \mathbf{a} = a_x\mathbf{i}+a_y\mathbf{j}
$$"] [17592186101947 :tutorial/content "The $\mathbf{i,j}$ notation can sometimes be cumbersome. An alternative is to use **angle bracket** notation. For example, using angle bracket notation, the vector $2\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}$ can be expressed as

$$
2\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}=\langle 2,3 \rangle
$$

Note that, using angle bracket notation, the special unit vectors can be expressed as

$$
i = 1i + 0j = ⟨1, 0⟩,; j = 0i + 1j = ⟨0, 1⟩
$$

We can also use **column vector** notation, which is similar to angle bracket notation but expresses the vector as a column rather than a row. For example, using column vector notation, the vector $2\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}
$$

Using column vector notation, the special unit vectors can be expressed as $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ and $\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$

**Note:** Sometimes, the round bracket notation $(\ldots)$ is used to denote vectors. However, we will avoid using that notation here, because it also looks like the coordinates of a point. A point and its position vector are two separate objects!"] [17592186101948 :tutorial/content "If $A$ and $B$ are points in the Cartesian plane with position vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ respectively, then

$$
\overrightarrow{AB} = \mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}
$$

To understand why the equation above is true, remember that

$$
\overrightarrow{OA} = \mathbf{a}
$$

and

$$
\overrightarrow{OB} = \mathbf{b}
$$

Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
AB^(→) &= AO^(→) + OB^(→) \\
&=-OA^(→) + OB^(→) \\
&=-a + b \\
&= b - a
\end{aligned}
$$

For example, given $A(5,13)$ and $B(-2,-35)$, we have

$$
OA^(→) = a = 5i + 13j,; OB^(→) = b =-2i - 35j
$$

Now, using the formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
AB^(→) &= b - a \\
&= (-2i - 35j) - (5i + 13j) \\
&=-7i - 48j
\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186060907 :tutorial/content "Suppose we are given two vectors

$$
\mathbf{a} = \langle 2,3 \rangle
$$

and

$$
\mathbf{b} = \langle -4,4 \rangle
$$

shown below. How do we compute the vectors $\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}$ and $-5\mathbf{a}$ in terms of the standard basis $\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}$?

![](images/25/254809cbc834b493759a6fa09222a2c90c5fbfc3280d22e82470e760a7a4c508.png)

To compute $\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}$, we collect all of the $\mathbf{i}$'s and $\mathbf{j}$'s. We know that

$$
\mathbf{a} = {\color{red}2}\mathbf{i} + {\color{blue}3}\mathbf{j}
$$

and

$$
\mathbf{b} = {\color{red}-4}\mathbf{i} + {\color{blue}4}\mathbf{j}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
a + b &= (2i + 3j) + (-4i + 4j) \\
&= (2 + (-4))i + (3 + 4)j \\
&=-2i + 7j
\end{aligned}
$$

Writing our answer in angle bracket and column vector notations, we get
$\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 7\end{bmatrix}$

To compute $-5\mathbf{a}$, we multiply each of the components by $-5$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
-5 \cdot a &= -5(2i + 3j) \\
&= (-5 \cdot 2)i + (-5 \cdot 3)j \\
&=-10i + - 15j
\end{aligned}
$$

Writing our answer in angle bracket and column vector notations, we get
$\begin{bmatrix}-10 \\ -15\end{bmatrix}$"] [17592186060908 :tutorial/content "To add or subtract vectors given in angle bracket or column vector form, we just need to add or subtract each component separately.

For example, in angle bracket notation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
⟨2, 5⟩ + ⟨- 3, 7⟩ &=  \\
⟨2 + (-3), 5 + 7⟩ &=  \\
&= ⟨- 1, 12⟩ \mid
\end{aligned}
$$

and in column vector notation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 5\end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 7\end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix}2 + (-3) \\ 5 + 7\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 12\end{bmatrix}
\end{aligned}
$$

Likewise, to multiply a vector given in angle bracket or column vector form, we just need to multiply each component separately.

For example, in angle bracket notation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
-5 \cdot ⟨2, 5⟩ &=  \\
⟨(-5) \cdot 2, (-5) \cdot 5⟩ &=  \\
&= ⟨- 10,-25⟩ \mid
\end{aligned}
$$

and in column vector notation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
-5 \cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 5\end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix}(-5) \cdot 2 \\ (-5) \cdot 5\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}-10 \\ -25\end{bmatrix}
\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186060909 :tutorial/content "To denote a vector, we have used two notations:

- a single bold lowercase letter, such as $\mathbf{v}$, or
- two uppercase letters representing the points of the ends of the vector, with an arrow over them, such as $\overrightarrow{AB}$.

We will mostly stick to these notations. However, there are many possible notations for vectors. For example, sometimes a vector can be denoted as
$\vec{v}, \quad \overrightarrow{V}, \quad v, \quad \hat{v}$.
The rightmost notation, $\hat{v}$, is usually used to represent unit vectors in particular."] [17592186060910 :tutorial/content "Consider the vector

$$
\mathbf{a}=\langle -2,4 \rangle
$$

shown below.

![](images/cd/cd458eeb41ee09d6a4f58bc343575d46e3d362dc3edca40a47e1a7381fcc9bd2.png)

Expressed in component form, our vector is

$$
\mathbf{a}=-2\mathbf{i} + 4 \mathbf{j}
$$

To find the magnitude (length) of $\mathbf{a}$, we can use the Pythagorean theorem on $\triangle OXA$.

The legs of the triangle have lengths

$$
\begin{aligned}
\begin{vmatrix}OX^(→) & &= \end{vmatrix}- 2|= 2
\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}
\begin{vmatrix}XA^(→) & &= \end{vmatrix}4|= 4
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the Pythagorean theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mid a \mid &= \sqrt{\begin{vmatrix}OX^(→) & ^{2} +\left.\end{vmatrix}XA^(→)\right|^{2}} \\
&= \sqrt{2^{2} + 4^{2}} \\
&= 2\sqrt{5}
\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186060911 :tutorial/content "We just saw that the magnitude of the vector

$$
\mathbf{a}=\langle -2,4 \rangle
$$

was given by

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mid a \mid &= \sqrt{(-2)^{2} + 4^{2}} \\
&= 2\sqrt{5}
\end{aligned}
$$

In general, given a vector
$\begin{bmatrix}a_{x} \\ a_{y}\end{bmatrix}$
the magnitude of the vector can always be computed as

$$
\mid \,\mathbf{a}\, \mid = \sqrt{a_x^2+a_y^2}
$$

:question/worked-solution "We will write the equation of the line in the slope-intercept form $y=mx+b.$ So we need to work out the slope $m$ and the $y$-intercept $b.$\n\nFrom the graph, we see that the line intercepts the $y$-axis at $(0,3).$ So, the $y$-intercept is $b=3.$\n\nWe can calculate the slope of the line by choosing two points on the line and applying the slope formula. The line passes through the points $(0,3)$ and $(2,0),$ so we calculate its slope as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}m & =\\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}} \\\\  & =\\frac{0-3}{2-0} \\\\  & =\\frac{-3}{2} \\\\  & =-\\frac{3}{2}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSubstituting the slope $m=-\\frac{3}{2}$ and the $y$-intercept $b=3$ into the slope-intercept form $y=mx+b,$ we obtain the equation of the line:\n\n$$\ny=-\\frac{3}{2}x+3\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186101010 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186100595 :question/id #uuid "8351e1cb-c602-5968-be5a-9c337ad977de" :question/worked-solution "We will write the equation of the line in the slope-intercept form $y=mx+b.$ So, we need to work out the slope $m$ and the $y$-intercept $b.$\n\nFirst, we calculate the slope $m$ using the given points:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}m & =\\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}} \\\\  & =\\frac{2-(-2)}{0-6} \\\\  & =\\frac{2+2}{0-6} \\\\  & =\\frac{4}{-6} \\\\  & =-\\frac{2}{3}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThe coordinates of the $y$-intercept are always $(0,b).$ We know that the line passes through the point $(0,2),$ so the $y$-intercept is $b=2.$  \n\nSubstituting the slope $m=-\\frac{2}{3}$ and the $y$-intercept $b=2$ into the slope-intercept formula $y=mx+b,$ we reach\n\n$$\ny=-\\frac{2}{3}x+2.\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186049394} {:db/id 17592186050095} {:db/id But what if two (or more) sides have the same length?\n\nAs you might have guessed, if two sides have the same length, then the opposite angles have the same measure. And vice-versa: if two angles have the same measure, then the opposite sides have the same length.\n\nSo, we obtain the following important properties of isosceles and equilateral triangles:\n\n- A triangle is **equilateral** if and only if all of its angles are of $60^\\circ.$\n\n![](images/ad/ad56532db83ae54eeabf04d5a182a850bed14d9d0a65518b8048c3c0c112c371.png)\n\n- A triangle is **isosceles** if and only if it has two congruent angles.\n\n![](images/2b/2b5d6779527eae10e108ffcdc80745f63f3f38e41474673990bf74c83d2e6a64.png)\n\n**Note:** The statement above encompasses two theorems:\n\n- The **isosceles triangle theorem**:\n\n*If a triangle is isosceles, then the base angles are congruent.*\n\n- The **converse isosceles triangle theorem**: \n\n*If two angles in a triangle have the same :step/content {:db/id 17592186070026 :tutorial/content "**Absolute value inequalities** combine two basic concepts: absolute value and inequality. The absolute value of a number is its distance from zero, while an inequality specifies a range of values.\n\nConsider a simple absolute value inequality, as follows:\n\n$$\n|x| < 7\n$$\n\nThis inequality specifies every number $x$ that is less than a distance of $7$ from $0$. So, it represents the same thing as the following compound inequality:\n\n$$\n-7 < x < 7\n$$\n\nTo solve an absolute value inequality, we first convert it to a compound inequality to remove the absolute value. Then, we can solve the compound inequality using the usual methods.\n\nTo illustrate, let's solve the following inequality:\n\n$$\n|2x+3| \\leq 5\n$$\n\nFirst, we interpret the inequality: the inequality specifies every number $2x+3$ whose distance from zero is less than or equal to $5.$ So, it represents the same thing as the following compound inequality:\n\n$$\n-5 \\leq 2x+3 \\leq 5\n$$\n\nNow, we can solve the compound inequality using the usual methods:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}-5\\le 2x+3\\le 5 \\\\ -8\\le 2x\\le 2 \\\\ -4\\le x\\le 1\\end{aligned}\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid :step/math-academy-id 15690 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097490}} {:db/id 17592186097473 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097830 :tutorial/content "Given a vector $\\overrightarrow{AB},$ the **opposite vector** is the vector $\\overrightarrow{BA}$ that has the same length but goes in the opposite direction.\n\n![](images/65/6591fd004ba2b74c2651182ce0c70302ac789d868389d057a502b8e98ac61fab.png)\n\nWe write\n\n$$\n\\overrightarrow{AB}=-\\overrightarrow{BA}.\n$$\n\nTo compute the sum of two opposite vectors,\n\n$$\n\\overrightarrow{AB}+\\overrightarrow{BA},\n$$\n\nwe can use the triangle law of addition.\n\nAccording to the triangle law of addition, the resultant is the vector that goes from the tail of $\\overrightarrow{AB}$ to the head of $\\overrightarrow{BA}.$ Therefore, we obtain a new vector for which the tail and head are the same point, $A.$ We denote that vector as\n\n$$\n\\overrightarrow{AB}+\\overrightarrow{BA} = \\overrightarrow{AA}=\\mathbf{0}.\n$$\n\nThe vector $\\mathbf{0}$ is called the **zero vector**. The zero vector has no direction and zero magnitude. of the line is $m={\\color{red}{2}},$ because a change of $1$ in the $x$-direction results in a change of $2$ in the $y$-direction.\n\n- The $y$*-intercept* of the line, denoted $b$, is $b={\\color{blue}{1}},$ because the line hits the $y$-axis at the point $(0,{\\color{blue}{1}}).$\n\n**Note**: The coordinates of the $y$-intercept are always $(0,{\\color{blue}{b}}).$\n\nFinally, if of the line by choosing two points on the line and applying the slope formula. The line passes through the points $(0,3)$ and $(2,0),$ so we calculate its slope as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}m & =\\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}} \\\\  & =\\frac{0-3}{2-0} \\\\  & =\\frac{-3}{2} \\\\  & =-\\frac{3}{2}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSubstituting the slope $m=-\\frac{3}{2}$ and the $y$-intercept $b=3$ into the slope-intercept form $y=mx+b,$ we obtain the equation of the We start by recalling the conversion table for mass units. \n\n| Name | Symbol | Conversion |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| Kilogram | $\\textrm{kg}$ | $1\\,\\textrm{kg} = 1\\,000\\,\\textrm{g}$ |\n| Gram | $\\textrm{g}$ | Base Unit |\n| Milligram | $\\textrm{mg}$ | $1\\,000\\,\\textrm{mg} = 1\\,\\textrm{g}$ |\n\nSince we're converting from kilograms to grams, we need a conversion between these two units. According to our table, there are $1000\\,\\textrm g$ per $\\textrm{kg}.$ We can write this ratio as a fraction, as follows:\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{1000\\,\\textrm g}{\\textrm{kg}}\n$$\n\nThis is our **conversion factor.** It's important to write the conversion factor with the units included.\n\nTo convert $0.03 \\,\\textrm{kg}$ to grams, we multiply this quantity by our conversion factor as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}0.03\\,\\text{kg} & =0.03\\,\\text{kg}\\cdot \\frac{1\\,000\\,\\text{g}}{\\text{kg}}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNotice that the kilogram units $(\\textrm{kg})$ cancel, leaving only gram units $(\\textrm{g}).$ Consequently, our expression can be simplified as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}0.03\\,\\text{kg} & =0.03\\,\\text{kg}\\cdot \\frac{1\\,000\\,\\text{g}}{\\text{kg}} \\\\  & =0.03\\,\\cancel{\\text{kg}}\\cdot \\frac{1\\,000\\,\\text{g}}{\\cancel{\\text{kg}}} \\\\  & =0.03\\cdot 1\\,000\\,\\text{g} \\\\  & =30\\,\\text{g}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, $0.03 \\,\\textrm{kg}$ is equivalent to $30 \\,\\text{g}.$\n\nNote the following:\n\n- When multiplying by the conversion factor, the units we want to remove should *always* cancel, and the units we wish to keep should *always* remain. If this isn't the case, we've made a mistake somewhere.\n\n- We can think of the conversion factor as equivalent to the number $1,$ and multiplying a quantity by $1$ doesn't change it. Therefore, multiplying $0.03\\,\\textrm{kg}$ by the conversion factor doesn't change the *size* of the quantity, though it does change the units.\n\nFinally, notice that, in this example, we've converted from a \"larger\" unit of mass $(\\textrm{kg})$ to a smaller one $(\\textrm{g}).$ We'll see how to use units to convert from smaller units of mass to larger units later in this lesson." \\,dϕ.\n$$\n\nIf $(\\rho ,\\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:\n\n$$\nx=\\rho \\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\\,y=\\rho \\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\\,z=\\rho \\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\n$$\n\nNotice that the region $R$ represents the sphere \\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\\rho \\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\\rho \\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\\\  & =3{e}^{({\\rho }^{2})^{3/2}} \\\\  & =3{e}^{{\\rho }^{3}}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}3{e}^{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})^{3}}\\,\\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}3{e}^{{\\rho }^{3}}\\cdot {\\rho }^{2}\\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\\,d\\rho \\,d\\theta \\,dϕ \\\\  & ={\\int }_{0}^{\\pi }{\\int }_{0}^{2\\pi }{\\int }_{0}^{1}3{\\rho }^{2}{e}^{{\\rho }^{3}}\\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\\,d\\rho \\,d\\theta \\,dϕ \\\\  & ={\\int }_{0}^{\\pi }\\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\\,dϕ\\cdot {\\int }_{0}^{2\\pi }d\\theta \\cdot {\\int }_{0}^{1}3{\\rho }^{2}{e}^{{\\rho }^{3}}\\,d\\rho  \\\\  & =[-\\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ]_{ϕ=0}^{ϕ=\\pi }\\cdot [\\theta ]_{\\theta =0}^{\\theta =2\\pi }\\cdot [{e}^{{\\rho }^{3}}]_{\\rho =0}^{\\rho =1}\\,d\\rho  \\\\  & =-(-1-1)\\cdot 17592186130203 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130455 :tutorial/content "When evaluating triple integrals, it's sometimes easier to change the variables from Cartesian coordinates to spherical polar coordinates.\n\nFor example, suppose we want to evaluate the triple integral\n\n$$\n\\displaystyle \\iiint\\limits_R \\left(x^2 + y^2 + z^2\\right)^{3/2} \\: \\textrm{d}V\n$$\n\nwhere $R$ is the region enclosed by the sphere of radius $1$ centered at $O,$ as shown below.\n\n![](images/08/0809a74f0aca2b3042b7f8db6783f9d6a13bc84bfc75ddcbb4d3076dbf0a2efd.png)\n\nThis integral seems too challenging when written in Cartesian coordinates. However, we should recognize that the problem lends itself to spherical polar coordinates because\n\n- the domain $R$ has a simple spherical polar representation, and\n\n- the integrand $f(x,y,z)=\\left(x^2+y^2+z^2\\right)^{3/2}$ can also be expressed simply in spherical polar coordinates.\n\nSo, let's transform the entire problem to spherical polar coordinates using the transformation $\\mathbf{T},$ defined by\n\n$$\nx = \\rho\\cos\\theta\\sin\\phi, \\qquad\n\ny = \\rho\\sin\\theta\\sin\\phi, \\qquad \n\nz = \\rho\\cos\\phi.\n$$\n\nThe preimage of $R$ under the action of $\\mathbf{T}$ is the rectangular region $\\Delta,$ given by\n\n$$\n\\Delta = \\left\\{ (\\rho, \\theta, \\phi) \\, : \\, 0 \\leq \\rho \\leq 1, \\: 0 \\leq \\theta \\lt 2\\pi, \\: 0 \\leq \\phi \\leq \\pi \\right\\},\n$$\n\nas shown below.\n\n![](images/c2/c2ed8a57c5e66687428a524eb148f96672f3a1ace7fbd28d426de065b2fb5f1f.png)\n\nTo express our integral in terms of spherical polar coordinates, we will use the change of variables formula\n\n$$\n\\iiint\\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \\, \\mathrm{d}V = \n\n\\iiint\\limits_{\\Delta} \\, f(\\rho\\cos\\theta\\sin\\phi, \\rho\\sin\\theta\\sin\\phi, \\rho\\cos\\phi) \\: \\left| \\dfrac{\\partial (x,y,z)}{\\partial (\\rho, \\theta, \\phi)} \\right| \\: \\mathrm{d}\\rho \\, \\mathrm{d}\\theta \\, \\mathrm{d}\\phi.\n$$\n\nIt can be shown that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant for a spherical change of variables is\n\n$$\n\\left| \\dfrac{\\partial (x,y,z)}{\\partial (\\rho, \\theta, \\phi)} \\right| = \\rho^2\\sin\\phi.\n$$\n\nTherefore, the change of variables formula is\n\n$$\n\\iiint\\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \\, \\mathrm{d}V = \n\n\\iiint\\limits_{\\Delta} \\, f(\\rho\\cos\\theta\\sin\\phi, \\rho\\sin\\theta\\sin\\phi, \\rho\\cos\\phi) \\:  \\rho^2\\sin\\phi \\: \\mathrm{d}\\rho \\, \\mathrm{d}\\theta \\, \\mathrm{d}\\phi.\n$$\n\nNow, let's write our function $f(x,y,z) = \\left(x^2 + y^2 + z^2\\right)^{3/2}$ in spherical polar coordinates:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\\rho \\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\\rho \\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\\rho \\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\\\  & ={({\\rho }^{2})}^{3/2} \\\\  & ={\\rho }^{3}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}^{3/2}\\,\\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}{\\rho }^{3}\\cdot {\\rho }^{2}\\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\\,d\\rho \\,d\\theta \\,dϕ \\\\  & ={\\int }_{0}^{\\pi }{\\int }_{0}^{2\\pi }{\\int }_{0}^{1}{\\rho }^{5}\\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\\,d\\rho \\,d\\theta \\,dϕ \\\\  & ={\\int }_{0}^{\\pi }\\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\\,dϕ\\cdot {\\int }_{0}^{2\\pi }d\\theta \\cdot {\\int }_{0}^{1}{\\rho }^{5}\\,d\\rho  \\\\  & =[-\\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ]_{ϕ=0}^{ϕ=\\pi }\\cdot [\\theta ]_{\\theta =0}^{\\theta =2\\pi }\\cdot {[\\frac{1}{6}{\\rho }^{6}]}_{\\rho =0}^{\\rho =1}\\,d\\rho  \\\\  & =-(-1-1)\\cdot (2\\pi -0)\\cdot \\frac{1}{6}(1-0) \\\\  & =2\\cdot 2\\pi \\cdot \\frac{1}{6} \\\\  & =\\frac{2\\pi }{3}.\\end{aligned}\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid 44584 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130205}} {:db/id 17592186130235 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130468 :tutorial/content "Throughout this lesson, we've used the fact that \n\n$$\n\\left| \\dfrac{\\partial (x, y, z)}{\\partial (\\rho, \\theta, \\phi)} \\right| = \\rho^2 \\sin{\\phi}.\n$$\n\nLet's now prove this result.\n\nGiven the spherical coordinate transformations\n\n$$\nx = \\rho\\cos\\theta\\sin\\phi, \\qquad\n\ny = \\rho\\sin\\theta\\sin\\phi, \\qquad \n\nz = \\rho\\cos\\phi,\n$$\n\nwe first  calculate the required partial derivatives:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂x}{∂\\rho } & =\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \\,\\frac{∂x}{∂\\theta } & =-\\rho \\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \\,\\frac{∂x}{∂ϕ} & =\\rho \\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ \\\\ \\frac{∂y}{∂\\rho } & =\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \\,\\frac{∂y}{∂\\theta } & =\\rho \\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \\,\\frac{∂y}{∂ϕ} & =\\rho \\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ \\\\ \\frac{∂z}{∂\\rho } & =\\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ & \\,\\frac{∂z}{∂\\theta } & =0 & \\,\\frac{∂z}{∂ϕ} & =-\\rho \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(\\rho ,\\theta ,ϕ)} & =|\\begin{aligned}\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & -\\rho \\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \\rho \\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ \\\\ \\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \\rho \\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \\rho \\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ \\\\ \\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ & 0 & -\\rho \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =\\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ|\\begin{aligned}-\\rho \\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \\rho \\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ \\\\ \\rho \\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \\rho \\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\\end{aligned}|-\\rho \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ|\\begin{aligned}\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & -\\rho \\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ \\\\ \\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \\rho \\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =\\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\\cdot (-{\\rho }^{2}\\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ({sin}^{2}⁡\\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\\theta ))-\\rho \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\\cdot \\rho {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\\cdot ({cos}^{2}⁡\\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\\theta ) \\\\  & =-{\\rho }^{2}\\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ{cos}^{2}⁡ϕ-{\\rho }^{2}\\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ \\\\  & =-{\\rho }^{2}\\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ({cos}^{2}⁡ϕ+{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ) \\\\  & =-{\\rho }^{2}\\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we conclude that\n\n$$\n\\left| \\dfrac{\\partial (x, y, z)}{\\partial (\\rho, \\theta, \\phi)} \\right| = \\rho^2 \\sin{\\phi}.\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "86bd6cae-b4e6-5da9-80b3-b884c320bda3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7720 :tutorial/title "Deriving the Jacobian for Spherical Polar Coordinates"} :step/id #uuid "96fb4483-0ca7-52c1-9f83-46c894da5471" :step/math-academy-id 44767 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130236}} {:db/id 17592186130236 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130469 :tutorial/content "We can also derive the change of variables formula for spherical polar coordinates using geometry.\n\nConsider a bounded spherical box $R,$ given by\n\n$$\nR = \\big\\{ (\\rho,\\theta,\\phi) \\: | \\: a \\leq \\rho \\leq b, \\:\\: \\alpha \\leq \\theta \\leq \\beta, \\:\\: \\gamma \\leq \\phi \\leq \\psi \\big\\}.\n$$\n\nWe can divide each interval into $l,m,$ and $n$ subdivisions such that \n\n$$\n\\Delta\\rho = \\dfrac{b-a}{l},\\qquad \\Delta\\theta = \\dfrac{\\beta-\\alpha}{m},\\qquad \\Delta\\phi = \\dfrac{\\psi-\\gamma}{n}.\n$$\n\nThis splits the region into \"spherical wedges,\" as shown in the following diagram.\n\n![](images/88/88be4c6a09062321d20ac7f48dfbb6be796cdd6b5bb1b7f6adc49a6ae1da609b.png)\n\nZooming in on one of these wedges, we obtain a shape resembling a rectangular solid.\n\n![](images/5e/5e5f7acb4d057e856c66e9d5626f81178ca26c0b7ce83cdf7290b1f4c64b1852.png)\n\nLet's note the volume of this solid as $\\Delta V.$ To approximate the value of $\\Delta V,$ we use the formula for the volume of a rectangular solid:\n\n$$\n\\Delta V \\approx lwh\n$$\n\nClearly, the height of the rectangular solid is $h = \\Delta \\rho.$ We can find the remaining dimensions using simple geometry. \n\nFirst, we need to find the length of the radius $r$ in the $xy$-plane. Using the following triangle and a side-on view of the wedge, we conclude that $r=\\rho\\sin\\phi.$\n\n![](images/01/0122c6c3b813bbe2821dbede794b6027cd69002dd1828925811211045a0d67e8.png)\n\nLet's add this to our diagram.\n\n![](images/d4/d41b538e9bb3add9bae1e3a24c9f87ae282a8b969f0c0dc4acd374ad777de74a.png)\n\nFinally, we can use the arc length formula $s = r \\cdot \\theta$ to find the length $l$ and width $w.$\n\n![](images/88/882b9243d1189c098aaf6e1e45ca7ec97d480b1f2c3a8fe23d5e39a6c2313ed2.png)\n\nThe length of our wedge is \n\n$$\nl = \\rho \\cdot \\Delta\\phi = \\rho\\Delta\\phi\n$$\n\n and the width is \n\n$$\nw = \\rho\\sin\\phi \\cdot \\Delta\\theta = \\rho\\sin\\phi\\Delta\\theta.\n$$\n\nCalculating the volume as a rectangular solid, we obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}ΔV & ≈lwh \\\\  & =(\\rho Δϕ)\\cdot (\\rho \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕΔ\\theta )\\cdot (Δ\\rho ) \\\\  & ={\\rho }^{2}\\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\\,Δϕ\\,Δ\\theta \\,Δ\\rho .\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nAs a result, we define the triple integral in spherical coordinates as the limit of a triple Riemann sum, where $(\\rho_{ijk},\\theta_{ijk},\\phi_{ijk})$ being any sample point in the spherical subregion $B{ijk}{:}$\n\n$$\n\\lim\\limits_{l,m,n \\to \\infty} \\sum\\limits_{i=1}^{l} \\sum\\limits_{j=1}^{m} \\sum\\limits_{k=1}^{n} f(\\rho_{ijk},\\theta_{ijk},\\phi_{ijk}) (\\rho_{ijk})^2 \\sin \\phi_{ijk} \\:\\Delta\\rho\\:\\Delta\\theta\\:\\Delta\\phi\n$$\n\nAs we increase the number of subregions, the size of $\\Delta\\rho,$ $\\Delta\\theta,$ and $\\Delta\\phi$ all goes to zero, and the volume of $R$ sometimes easier to change the variables from Cartesian coordinates to spherical polar coordinates.\n\nFor example, suppose we want to evaluate the triple integral\n\n$$\n\\displaystyle \\iiint\\limits_R \\left(x^2 + y^2 + z^2\\right)^{3/2} \\: \\textrm{d}V\n$$\n\nwhere $R$ is the region enclosed by the sphere of radius $1$ centered at $O,$ as shown below.\n\n![](images/08/0809a74f0aca2b3042b7f8db6783f9d6a13bc84bfc75ddcbb4d3076dbf0a2efd.png)\n\nThis integral seems too challenging when written in Cartesian coordinates. However, we should recognize that the problem lends itself to spherical polar coordinates because\n\n- the domain $R$ has a simple spherical polar representation, and\n\n- the integrand $f(x,y,z)=\\left(x^2+y^2+z^2\\right)^{3/2}$ can also be expressed simply in spherical polar coordinates.\n\nSo, let's transform the entire problem to spherical polar coordinates using the transformation $\\mathbf{T},$ defined by\n\n$$\nx = \\rho\\cos\\theta\\sin\\phi, \\qquad\n\ny = \\rho\\sin\\theta\\sin\\phi, \\qquad \n\nz = \\rho\\cos\\phi.\n$$\n\nThe preimage of $R$ under the action of $\\mathbf{T}$ is the rectangular region $\\Delta,$ given by\n\n$$\n\\Delta = \\left\\{ (\\rho, \\theta, \\phi) \\, : \\, 0 \\leq \\rho \\leq 1, \\: 0 \\leq \\theta \\lt 2\\pi, \\: 0 \\leq \\phi \\leq \\pi \\right\\},\n$$\n\nas shown below.\n\n![](images/c2/c2ed8a57c5e66687428a524eb148f96672f3a1ace7fbd28d426de065b2fb5f1f.png)\n\nTo express our integral in terms of spherical polar \\mathrm{d}\\phi.\n$$\n\nIt can be shown that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant for a spherical change of variables is\n\n$$\n\\left| \\dfrac{\\partial (x,y,z)}{\\partial (\\rho, \\theta, \\phi)} \\right| = \\rho^2\\sin\\phi.\n$$\n\nTherefore, the change of variables formula is\n\n$$\n\\iiint\\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \\, \\mathrm{d}V = \n\n\\iiint\\limits_{\\Delta} \\, f(\\rho\\cos\\theta\\sin\\phi, \\rho\\sin\\theta\\sin\\phi, \\rho\\cos\\phi) \\:  \\rho^2\\sin\\phi \\: \\mathrm{d}\\rho \\, \\mathrm{d}\\theta \\, \\mathrm{d}\\phi.\n$$\n\nNow, let's write our function $f(x,y,z) = \\left(x^2 + y^2 + z^2\\right)^{3/2}$ in spherical polar coordinates:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\\rho \\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\\rho formula, we obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}^{3/2}\\,\\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}{\\rho }^{3}\\cdot {\\rho }^{2}\\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\\,d\\rho \\,d\\theta \\,dϕ \\\\  & }d\\theta \\cdot {\\int }_{0}^{1}{\\rho }^{5}\\,d\\rho  \\\\  & =[-\\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ]_{ϕ=0}^{ϕ=\\pi }\\cdot [\\theta ]_{\\theta =0}^{\\theta =2\\pi }\\cdot {[\\frac{1}{6}{\\rho }^{6}]}_{\\rho =0}^{\\rho =1}\\,d\\rho  \\\\  & =-(-1-1)\\cdot (2\\pi -0)\\cdot \\frac{1}{6}(1-0) \\\\  & =2\\cdot 2\\pi \\cdot \\frac{1}{6} \\\\  & =\\frac{2\\pi }{3}.\\end{aligned}\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid prove this result.\n\nGiven the spherical coordinate transformations\n\n$$\nx = \\rho\\cos\\theta\\sin\\phi, \\qquad\n\ny = \\rho\\sin\\theta\\sin\\phi, \\qquad \n\nz = \\rho\\cos\\phi,\n$$\n\nwe first  calculate the required partial derivatives:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂x}{∂\\rho } & =\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \\,\\frac{∂x}{∂\\theta } & =-\\rho \\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \\,\\frac{∂x}{∂ϕ} & =\\rho \\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ \\\\ \\frac{∂y}{∂\\rho } & =\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \\,\\frac{∂y}{∂\\theta } & =\\rho \\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \\,\\frac{∂y}{∂ϕ} & =\\rho \\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ \\\\ \\frac{∂z}{∂\\rho } & =\\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ & \\,\\frac{∂z}{∂\\theta } & =0 & \\,\\frac{∂z}{∂ϕ} & =-\\rho \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(\\rho ,\\theta ,ϕ)} & =|\\begin{aligned}\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & -\\rho \\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \\rho \\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ \\\\ \\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \\rho \\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \\rho \\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ \\\\ \\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ & 0 & -\\rho \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =\\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ|\\begin{aligned}-\\rho \\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \\rho \\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ \\\\ \\rho \\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \\rho \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ \\\\ \\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \\rho \\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =\\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\\cdot (-{\\rho }^{2}\\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ({sin}^{2}⁡\\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\\theta ))-\\rho \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\\cdot \\rho {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\\cdot ({cos}^{2}⁡\\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\\theta ) \\\\  & =-{\\rho }^{2}\\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ{cos}^{2}⁡ϕ-{\\rho }^{2}\\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ \\\\  & =-{\\rho }^{2}\\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ({cos}^{2}⁡ϕ+{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ) \\\\  & =-{\\rho }^{2}\\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we conclude that\n\n$$\n\\left| \\dfrac{\\partial (x, y, z)}{\\partial (\\rho, \\theta, \\phi)} \\right| = \\rho^2 \\sin{\\phi}.\n$$" $l,m,$ and $n$ subdivisions such that \n\n$$\n\\Delta\\rho = \\dfrac{b-a}{l},\\qquad \\Delta\\theta = \\dfrac{\\beta-\\alpha}{m},\\qquad \\Delta\\phi = \\dfrac{\\psi-\\gamma}{n}.\n$$\n\nThis splits the region into \"spherical wedges,\" as shown in the following diagram.\n\n![](images/88/88be4c6a09062321d20ac7f48dfbb6be796cdd6b5bb1b7f6adc49a6ae1da609b.png)\n\nZooming in on one of these wedges, we obtain a shape resembling a rectangular solid.\n\n![](images/5e/5e5f7acb4d057e856c66e9d5626f81178ca26c0b7ce83cdf7290b1f4c64b1852.png)\n\nLet's note the volume of this solid as $\\Delta V.$ To approximate the value of $\\Delta V,$ we use the formula for the volume of a rectangular solid:\n\n$$\n\\Delta V \\approx lwh\n$$\n\nClearly, the height of the rectangular solid is $h = \\Delta :question/worked-solution "We will use the change of variables formula in the form\n\n$$\n{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\\,f(\\rho \\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\\rho \\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\\rho \\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\\,{\\rho }^{2}\\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\\,d\\rho \\,d\\theta \\,dϕ.\n$$\n\nIf $(\\rho ,\\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:\n\n$$\nx=\\rho \\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\\,y=\\rho \\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\\,z=\\rho \\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\n$$\n\nNotice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $2$ centered at the origin. \nAs a result, in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as \n\n$$\nΔ=\\{(\\rho ,\\theta ,ϕ)\\,:\\,0\\le \\rho \\le 2,\\,0\\le \\theta \\le 2\\pi ,\\,0\\le ϕ\\le \\pi \\}.\n$$\n\nNext, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)={z}^{2}:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\\rho \\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\\rho \\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\\rho \\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\\\  & =(\\rho \\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\\\  & ={\\rho }^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡ϕ\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}z\\,\\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}{\\rho }^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡ϕ\\cdot {\\rho }^{2}\\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\\,d\\rho \\,d\\theta \\,dϕ \\\\  & ={\\int }_{0}^{\\pi }{\\int }_{0}^{2\\pi }{\\int }_{0}^{2}{\\rho }^{4}{cos}^{2}⁡ϕ\\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\\,d\\rho \\,d\\theta \\,dϕ \\\\  & ={\\int }_{0}^{\\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡ϕ\\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\\,dϕ\\cdot {\\int }_{0}^{2\\pi }d\\theta \\cdot {\\int }_{0}^{2}{\\rho }^{4}\\,d\\rho  \\\\  & ={[-\\frac{1}{3}{cos}^{3}⁡ϕ]}_{ϕ=0}^{ϕ=\\pi }\\cdot [\\theta ]_{\\theta =0}^{\\theta =2\\pi }\\cdot {[\\frac{1}{5}{\\rho }^{5}]}_{\\rho =0}^{\\rho =2}\\,d\\rho  \\\\  & =-\\frac{1}{3}(-1-1)\\cdot (2\\pi -0)\\cdot \\frac{1}{5}(32-0) \\\\  & =\\frac{2}{3}\\cdot 2\\pi \\cdot \\frac{32}{5} \\\\  & =\\frac{128\\pi }{15}\\end{aligned}\n$$"} coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:\n\n$$\nx=\\rho \\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\\,y=\\rho \\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\\,z=\\rho \\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\n$$\n\nNotice that the region $R$ represents one-half of the sphere of radius $\\sqrt{2}$ centered at the }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ({cos}^{2}⁡\\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\\theta )} \\\\  & =\\rho \\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\\sqrt{{\\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ} \\\\  & ={\\rho }^{2}\\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}z\\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\\,\\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}{\\rho }^{2}\\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\\cdot {\\rho }^{2}\\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\\,d\\rho \\,d\\theta \\,dϕ \\\\  & ={\\int }_{0}^{\\pi }{\\int }_{\\pi }^{2\\pi }{\\int coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:\n\n$$\nx=\\rho \\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\\,y=\\rho \\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\\,z=\\rho \\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\n$$\n\nNotice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $\\sqrt{5}$ centered at the origin. \nAs a result, in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as \n\n$$\nΔ=\\{(\\rho ,\\theta ,ϕ)\\,:\\,0\\le \\rho \\le \\sqrt{5},\\,0\\le \\theta \\le 2\\pi ,\\,0\\le ϕ\\le \\pi \\}.\n$$\n\nNext, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=(x+z)\\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\\rho \\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\\rho \\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\\rho \\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\\\  & =(\\rho \\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ+\\rho \\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\\cdot \\rho  \\\\  & ={\\rho }^{2}(\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ+\\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}(x+z)\\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\\,\\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}{\\rho }^{2}(\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ+\\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\\cdot {\\rho }^{2}\\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\\,d\\rho \\,d\\theta \\,dϕ \\\\  & ={\\int }_{0}^{\\pi }{\\int }_{0}^{2\\pi }{\\int }_{0}^{\\sqrt{5}}{\\rho }^{4}\\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ(\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ+\\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\\,d\\rho \\,d\\theta \\,dϕ.\\end{aligned}\n$$"} :step/id #uuid
